1|## Installation
2|
3|Installation is as simple as:
4|
5|```bash
6|pip install pydantic-settings
7|```
8|
9|## Usage
10|
11|If you create a model that inherits from `BaseSettings`, the model initialiser will attempt to determine
12|the values of any fields not passed as keyword arguments by reading from the environment. (Default values
13|will still be used if the matching environment variable is not set.)
14|
15|This makes it easy to:
16|
17|* Create a clearly-defined, type-hinted application configuration class
18|* Automatically read modifications to the configuration from environment variables
19|* Manually override specific settings in the initialiser where desired (e.g. in unit tests)
20|
21|For example:
22|
23|```py
24|from collections.abc import Callable
25|from typing import Any
26|
27|from pydantic import (
28|    AliasChoices,
29|    AmqpDsn,
30|    BaseModel,
31|    Field,
32|    ImportString,
33|    PostgresDsn,
34|    RedisDsn,
35|)
36|
37|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
38|
39|
40|class SubModel(BaseModel):
41|    foo: str = 'bar'
42|    apple: int = 1
43|
44|
45|class Settings(BaseSettings):
46|    auth_key: str = Field(validation_alias='my_auth_key')  # (1)!
47|
48|    api_key: str = Field(alias='my_api_key')  # (2)!
49|
50|    redis_dsn: RedisDsn = Field(
51|        'redis://user:pass@localhost:6379/1',
52|        validation_alias=AliasChoices('service_redis_dsn', 'redis_url'),  # (3)!
53|    )
54|    pg_dsn: PostgresDsn = 'postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/foobar'
55|    amqp_dsn: AmqpDsn = 'amqp://user:pass@localhost:5672/'
56|
57|    special_function: ImportString[Callable[[Any], Any]] = 'math.cos'  # (4)!
58|
59|    # to override domains:
60|    # export my_prefix_domains='["foo.com", "bar.com"]'
61|    domains: set[str] = set()
62|
63|    # to override more_settings:
64|    # export my_prefix_more_settings='{"foo": "x", "apple": 1}'
65|    more_settings: SubModel = SubModel()
66|
67|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix='my_prefix_')  # (5)!
68|
69|
70|print(Settings().model_dump())
71|"""
72|{
73|    'auth_key': 'xxx',
74|    'api_key': 'xxx',
75|    'redis_dsn': RedisDsn('redis://user:pass@localhost:6379/1'),
76|    'pg_dsn': PostgresDsn('postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/foobar'),
77|    'amqp_dsn': AmqpDsn('amqp://user:pass@localhost:5672/'),
78|    'special_function': math.cos,
79|    'domains': set(),
80|    'more_settings': {'foo': 'bar', 'apple': 1},
81|}
82|"""
83|```
84|
85|1. The environment variable name is overridden using `validation_alias`. In this case, the environment variable
86|   `my_auth_key` will be read instead of `auth_key`.
87|
88|    Check the [`Field` documentation](fields.md) for more information.
89|
90|2. The environment variable name is overridden using `alias`. In this case, the environment variable
91|   `my_api_key` will be used for both validation and serialization instead of `api_key`.
92|
93|    Check the [`Field` documentation](fields.md#field-aliases) for more information.
94|
95|3. The [`AliasChoices`][pydantic.AliasChoices] class allows you to have multiple environment variable names for a single field.
96|   The first environment variable that is found will be used.
97|
98|    Check the [documentation on alias choices](alias.md#aliaspath-and-aliaschoices) for more information.
99|
100|4. The [`ImportString`][pydantic.types.ImportString] class allows you to import an object from a string.
101|   In this case, the environment variable `special_function` will be read and the function [`math.cos`][] will be imported.
102|
103|5. The `env_prefix` config setting allows you to set a prefix for all environment variables.
104|
105|    Check the [Environment variable names documentation](#environment-variable-names) for more information.
106|
107|## Validation of default values
108|
109|Unlike pydantic `BaseModel`, default values of `BaseSettings` fields are validated by default.
110|You can disable this behaviour by setting `validate_default=False` either in `model_config`
111|or on field level by `Field(validate_default=False)`:
112|
113|```py
114|from pydantic import Field
115|
116|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
117|
118|
119|class Settings(BaseSettings):
120|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(validate_default=False)
121|
122|    # default won't be validated
123|    foo: int = 'test'
124|
125|
126|print(Settings())
127|#> foo='test'
128|
129|
130|class Settings1(BaseSettings):
131|    # default won't be validated
132|    foo: int = Field('test', validate_default=False)
133|
134|
135|print(Settings1())
136|#> foo='test'
137|```
138|
139|Check the [validation of default values](fields.md#validate-default-values) for more information.
140|
141|## Runtime validation arguments
142|
143|`BaseSettings` defines a custom `__init__` to load values from settings sources, so `model_validate()`,
144|`model_validate_json()` and `model_validate_strings()` build the instance by calling that `__init__`.
145|As a consequence:
146|
147|* Settings sources are still applied, so values from environment variables, dotenv files, etc. are loaded
148|  just as when calling `Settings()`.
149|* Runtime validation arguments such as `extra`, `strict` and `context` are **not** applied. Validation uses
150|  the behaviour from `model_config` instead (for example, the default `extra='forbid'`).
151|
152|If you need different behaviour, set it in `model_config` or prepare the input data before validating.
153|For example, to build a parent settings class from an instance of a subclass, keep only the parent's fields:
154|
155|```py
156|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
157|
158|
159|class BaseAppSettings(BaseSettings):
160|    name: str = 'app'
161|
162|
163|class AppSettings(BaseAppSettings):
164|    debug: bool = False
165|
166|
167|settings = AppSettings(debug=True)
168|
169|# `extra='ignore'` is not applied here, so `debug` is rejected as an extra input:
170|# BaseAppSettings.model_validate(settings.model_dump(), extra='ignore')
171|
172|fields = BaseAppSettings.model_fields
173|data = {k: v for k, v in settings.model_dump().items() if k in fields}
174|print(BaseAppSettings.model_validate(data))
175|#> name='app'
176|```
177|
178|## Environment variable names
179|
180|By default, the environment variable name is the same as the field name.
181|
182|You can change the prefix for all environment variables by setting the `env_prefix` config setting,
183|or via the `_env_prefix` keyword argument on instantiation:
184|
185|```py
186|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
187|
188|
189|class Settings(BaseSettings):
190|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix='my_prefix_')
191|
192|    auth_key: str = 'xxx'  # will be read from `my_prefix_auth_key`
193|```
194|
195|!!! note
196|    The default `env_prefix` is `''` (empty string). `env_prefix` is not only for env settings but also for
197|    dotenv files, secrets, and other sources.
198|
199|If you want to change the environment variable name for a single field, you can use an alias.
200|
201|There are two ways to do this:
202|
203|* Using `Field(alias=...)` (see `api_key` above)
204|* Using `Field(validation_alias=...)` (see `auth_key` above)
205|
206|Check the [`Field` aliases documentation](fields.md#field-aliases) for more information about aliases.
207|
208|!!! note
209|    By default, setting an alias on a nested model field *narrows* which environment variables can reach it: its
210|    sub-fields are then looked up using only that alias as the prefix, in every source. The field's own name
211|    is not accepted as a lookup prefix unless `populate_by_name=True` (or `validate_by_name=True`) is enabled,
212|    including for dotenv files and other non-env sources.
213|
214|    This matters most when sources disagree on naming. If a higher-priority source uses the alias and a
215|    lower-priority one uses the field name, only the alias-based values are found — the others were never
216|    associated with the field, so there is nothing to merge and the lower-priority values appear to be
217|    ignored. What happens to them depends on `extra`: with the default `extra='forbid'` an unmatched dotenv
218|    entry is kept as an extra input and raises a `ValidationError`, while a plain environment variable is
219|    simply not picked up; with `extra='ignore'` both are dropped silently.
220|
221|    To accept both spellings, widen the set of accepted names — either globally with `populate_by_name=True`
222|    (or `validate_by_name=True`), or per field with [`AliasChoices`][pydantic.AliasChoices]. Both let
223|    mixed-naming sources merge:
224|
225|    ```py
226|    import os
227|    from pathlib import Path
228|
229|    from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
230|
231|    from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
232|
233|
234|    class SubModel(BaseModel):
235|        var1: str | None = None
236|        var2: str | None = None
237|
238|
239|    class Settings(BaseSettings):
240|        model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter='_', populate_by_name=True)
241|        submodel: SubModel | None = Field(alias='SUB', default=None)
242|
243|
244|    dotenv_file = Path('example.env')
245|    dotenv_file.write_text("SUBMODEL_VAR2='var2 from dotenv'")
246|    os.environ['SUB_VAR1'] = 'var1 from env'
247|
248|    print(Settings(_env_file=dotenv_file).model_dump())
249|    #> {'submodel': {'var1': 'var1 from env', 'var2': 'var2 from dotenv'}}
250|    dotenv_file.unlink(missing_ok=True)
251|    del os.environ['SUB_VAR1']
252|    ```
253|
254|    `AliasChoices` is often the better fit when only some fields need both spellings — for example a
255|    configuration file that spells section names out in full alongside abbreviated environment variables.
256|    It states per field exactly which names are accepted, instead of accepting every field name globally,
257|    and lets you opt each nesting level into both spellings independently:
258|
259|    ```py
260|    import os
261|    from pathlib import Path
262|
263|    from pydantic import AliasChoices, BaseModel, Field
264|
265|    from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
266|
267|
268|    class SubModel(BaseModel):
269|        var1: str | None = None
270|        var2: str | None = None
271|
272|
273|    class Settings(BaseSettings):
274|        model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter='_')
275|        submodel: SubModel | None = Field(
276|            validation_alias=AliasChoices('SUB', 'SUBMODEL'), default=None
277|        )
278|
279|
280|    dotenv_file = Path('example.env')
281|    dotenv_file.write_text("SUBMODEL_VAR2='var2 from dotenv'")
282|    os.environ['SUB_VAR1'] = 'var1 from env'
283|
284|    print(Settings(_env_file=dotenv_file).model_dump())
285|    #> {'submodel': {'var1': 'var1 from env', 'var2': 'var2 from dotenv'}}
286|    dotenv_file.unlink(missing_ok=True)
287|    del os.environ['SUB_VAR1']
288|    ```
289|
290|### Unknown environment variables
291|
292|Environment variables that do not match a settings field or its alias are ignored, even if they start
293|with `env_prefix` and `extra='forbid'` is set. The `extra` setting validates inputs passed to the model;
294|it does not check every name in `os.environ`. A misspelled field name can therefore leave a default
295|value in use without raising an error:
296|
297|```py
298|import os
299|
300|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
301|
302|
303|class Settings(BaseSettings):
304|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix='APP_', extra='forbid')
305|    port: int = 5432
306|
307|
308|os.environ['APP_PRT'] = '6543'  # (1)!
309|print(Settings().port)
310|#> 5432
311|del os.environ['APP_PRT']
312|```
313|
314|1. Misspelled, so it matches no field and is dropped before validation runs.
315|
316|The same applies to nested models: an incorrect `env_nested_delimiter` keeps the variable from matching
317|a field. Once a variable *does* match a known field's nested prefix, however, its contents are passed to
318|that field for validation, so an unknown key inside a nested model can raise a `ValidationError` if that
319|nested model has `extra='forbid'`:
320|
321|```py
322|import os
323|
324|from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError
325|
326|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
327|
328|
329|class Database(BaseModel):
330|    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
331|    port: int = 5432
332|
333|
334|class Settings(BaseSettings):
335|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
336|        env_prefix='APP_', env_nested_delimiter='__', extra='forbid'
337|    )
338|    database: Database = Database()
339|
340|
341|# A single underscore does not match the database field's nested prefix.
342|os.environ['APP_DATABASE_PORT'] = '6543'
343|print(Settings().database.port)
344|#> 5432
345|del os.environ['APP_DATABASE_PORT']
346|
347|# The nested prefix matches, so the unknown key reaches Database's validation.
348|os.environ['APP_DATABASE__PRT'] = '6543'
349|try:
350|    Settings()
351|except ValidationError as exc:
352|    print(exc.errors()[0]['type'])
353|    #> extra_forbidden
354|del os.environ['APP_DATABASE__PRT']
355|```
356|
357|For extra variables loaded from `.env` files and the effect of `dotenv_filtering`, see
358|[Dotenv (.env) support](#dotenv-env-support).
359|
360|### Environment variable prefix targets
361|
362|To apply `env_prefix` not only to variable names but also to aliases, set `env_prefix_target='all'`.
363|To apply `env_prefix` only to aliases and not to variable names, set `env_prefix_target='alias'`.
364|To apply `env_prefix` only to variable names (the default behavior), set `env_prefix_target='variable'`.
365|
366|
367|```py
368|import os
369|
370|from pydantic import Field
371|
372|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
373|
374|
375|class FooBarSettings(BaseSettings):
376|    # default
377|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix='TARGET_')
378|    foo: str = Field(alias='FooAlias')
379|    bar: str
380|
381|
382|os.environ['FooAlias'] = 'TARGET_FOO_VALUE'  # (1)!
383|os.environ['TARGET_BAR'] = 'TARGET_BAR_VALUE'
384|print(FooBarSettings().model_dump())
385|#> {'foo': 'TARGET_FOO_VALUE', 'bar': 'TARGET_BAR_VALUE'}
386|
387|
388|class TargetAllSettings(FooBarSettings):
389|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
390|        env_prefix='TARGET_ALL_',
391|        env_prefix_target='all',
392|    )
393|
394|
395|os.environ['TARGET_ALL_FooAlias'] = 'TARGET_ALL_FOO_VALUE'
396|os.environ['TARGET_ALL_BAR'] = 'TARGET_ALL_BAR_VALUE'
397|print(TargetAllSettings().model_dump())
398|#> {'foo': 'TARGET_ALL_FOO_VALUE', 'bar': 'TARGET_ALL_BAR_VALUE'}
399|
400|
401|class TargetAliasSettings(FooBarSettings):
402|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
403|        env_prefix='TARGET_ALIAS_',
404|        env_prefix_target='alias',
405|    )
406|
407|
408|os.environ['TARGET_ALIAS_FooAlias'] = 'TARGET_ALIAS_FOO_VALUE'
409|os.environ['BAR'] = 'TARGET_ALL_BAR_VALUE'
410|print(TargetAliasSettings().model_dump())
411|#> {'foo': 'TARGET_ALIAS_FOO_VALUE', 'bar': 'TARGET_ALL_BAR_VALUE'}
412|
413|
414|class TargetVarSettings(FooBarSettings):
415|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
416|        env_prefix='TARGET_VAR_',
417|        env_prefix_target='variable',
418|    )
419|
420|
421|os.environ['FooAlias'] = 'TARGET_VAR_FOO_VALUE'  # (1)!
422|os.environ['TARGET_VAR_BAR'] = 'TARGET_VAR_BAR_VALUE'
423|print(TargetVarSettings().model_dump())
424|#> {'foo': 'TARGET_VAR_FOO_VALUE', 'bar': 'TARGET_VAR_BAR_VALUE'}
425|```
426|
427|1. `env_prefix` will be ignored and the value will be read from `FooAlias` environment variable.
428|
429|The same applies to an alias on a nested model field:
430|
431|```py
432|import os
433|
434|from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
435|
436|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
437|
438|
439|class SubModel(BaseModel):
440|    var1: str | None = None
441|
442|
443|class NestedSettings(BaseSettings):
444|    # default
445|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix='APP_', env_nested_delimiter='_')
446|    submodel: SubModel | None = Field(alias='SUB', default=None)
447|
448|
449|os.environ['APP_SUB_VAR1'] = 'ignored'  # (1)!
450|print(NestedSettings().model_dump())
451|#> {'submodel': {'var1': None}}
452|del os.environ['APP_SUB_VAR1']
453|
454|os.environ['SUB_VAR1'] = 'unprefixed alias value'
455|print(NestedSettings().model_dump())
456|#> {'submodel': {'var1': 'unprefixed alias value'}}
457|del os.environ['SUB_VAR1']
458|
459|
460|class NestedTargetAllSettings(NestedSettings):
461|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
462|        env_prefix='APP_',
463|        env_nested_delimiter='_',
464|        env_prefix_target='all',
465|    )
466|
467|
468|os.environ['APP_SUB_VAR1'] = 'prefixed alias value'
469|print(NestedTargetAllSettings().model_dump())
470|#> {'submodel': {'var1': 'prefixed alias value'}}
471|del os.environ['APP_SUB_VAR1']
472|```
473|
474|1. `env_prefix` will be ignored and the alias is looked up under `SUB_VAR1`, not `APP_SUB_VAR1`.
475|
476|### Case-sensitivity
477|
478|By default, environment variable names are case-insensitive.
479|
480|If you want to make environment variable names case-sensitive, you can set the `case_sensitive` config setting:
481|
482|```py
483|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
484|
485|
486|class Settings(BaseSettings):
487|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(case_sensitive=True)
488|
489|    redis_host: str = 'localhost'
490|```
491|
492|When `case_sensitive` is `True`, the environment variable names must match field names (optionally with a prefix),
493|so in this example `redis_host` could only be modified via `export redis_host`. If you want to name environment variables
494|all upper-case, you should name attribute all upper-case too. You can still name environment variables anything
495|you like through `Field(validation_alias=...)`.
496|
497|Case-sensitivity can also be set via the `_case_sensitive` keyword argument on instantiation.
498|
499|In case of nested models, the `case_sensitive` setting will be applied to all nested models.
500|
501|```py
502|import os
503|
504|from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
505|
506|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
507|
508|
509|class RedisSettings(BaseModel):
510|    host: str
511|    port: int
512|
513|
514|class Settings(BaseSettings, case_sensitive=True):
515|    redis: RedisSettings
516|
517|
518|os.environ['redis'] = '{"host": "localhost", "port": 6379}'
519|print(Settings().model_dump())
520|#> {'redis': {'host': 'localhost', 'port': 6379}}
521|os.environ['redis'] = '{"HOST": "localhost", "port": 6379}'  # (1)!
522|try:
523|    Settings()
524|except ValidationError as e:
525|    print(e)
526|    """
527|    1 validation error for Settings
528|    redis.host
529|      Field required [type=missing, input_value={'HOST': 'localhost', 'port': 6379}, input_type=dict]
530|        For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2/v/missing
531|    """
532|```
533|
534|1. Note that the `host` field is not found because the environment variable name is `HOST` (all upper-case).
535|
536|!!! note
537|    On Windows, environment variable names exposed through Python's `os` module are case-insensitive
538|    and normalized to upper-case (e.g. setting `redis` results in `REDIS`). Because the original case
539|    cannot be recovered, the `case_sensitive` setting has **no effect for environment variables** on
540|    Windows — they are always matched ignoring case.
541|
542|    This only applies to environment variables. Values loaded from dotenv (`.env`) files preserve
543|    case, so `case_sensitive=True` is still respected for those, including on Windows.
544|
545|## Parsing environment variable values
546|
547|By default environment variables are parsed verbatim, including if the value is empty. You can choose to
548|ignore empty environment variables by setting the `env_ignore_empty` config setting to `True`. This can be
549|useful if you would prefer to use the default value for a field rather than an empty value from the
550|environment.
551|
552|For most simple field types (such as `int`, `float`, `str`, etc.), the environment variable value is parsed
553|the same way it would be if passed directly to the initialiser (as a string).
554|
555|Complex types like `list`, `set`, `dict`, and sub-models are populated from the environment by treating the
556|environment variable's value as a JSON-encoded string.
557|
558|!!! warning
559|    Because these values are JSON-decoded, an environment variable whose value is not valid JSON raises a
560|    [`SettingsError`](../api/pydantic_settings.md#pydantic_settings.SettingsError). For example, `NUMBERS=1,2,3`
561|    for a `numbers: list[int]` field fails, because `1,2,3` is not valid JSON. See
562|    [Disabling JSON parsing](#disabling-json-parsing) if you want to parse such values with your own logic.
563|
564|Another way to populate nested complex variables is to configure your model with the `env_nested_delimiter`
565|config setting, then use an environment variable with a name pointing to the nested module fields.
566|What it does is simply explodes your variable into nested models or dicts.
567|So if you define a variable `FOO__BAR__BAZ=123` it will convert it into `FOO={'BAR': {'BAZ': 123}}`
568|If you have multiple variables with the same structure they will be merged.
569|
570|!!! note
571|    Sub model has to inherit from `pydantic.BaseModel`, Otherwise `pydantic-settings` will initialize sub model,
572|    collects values for sub model fields separately, and you may get unexpected results.
573|
574|!!! note
575|    The `env_nested_delimiter` option applies to variables that match a declared top-level field's
576|    name or alias. Unknown keys within that field's nested value are still subject to the nested
577|    model's validation. See [Unknown environment variables](#unknown-environment-variables).
578|
579|As an example, given the following environment variables:
580|```bash
581|# your environment
582|export V0=0
583|export SUB_MODEL='{"v1": "json-1", "v2": "json-2"}'
584|export SUB_MODEL__V2=nested-2
585|export SUB_MODEL__V3=3
586|export SUB_MODEL__DEEP__V4=v4
587|```
588|
589|You could load them into the following settings model:
590|
591|```py
592|from pydantic import BaseModel
593|
594|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
595|
596|
597|class DeepSubModel(BaseModel):  # (1)!
598|    v4: str
599|
600|
601|class SubModel(BaseModel):  # (2)!
602|    v1: str
603|    v2: bytes
604|    v3: int
605|    deep: DeepSubModel
606|
607|
608|class Settings(BaseSettings):
609|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter='__')
610|
611|    v0: str
612|    sub_model: SubModel
613|
614|
615|print(Settings().model_dump())
616|"""
617|{
618|    'v0': '0',
619|    'sub_model': {'v1': 'json-1', 'v2': b'nested-2', 'v3': 3, 'deep': {'v4': 'v4'}},
620|}
621|"""
622|```
623|
624|1. Sub model has to inherit from `pydantic.BaseModel`.
625|
626|2. Sub model has to inherit from `pydantic.BaseModel`.
627|
628|`env_nested_delimiter` can be configured via the `model_config` as shown above, or via the
629|`_env_nested_delimiter` keyword argument on instantiation.
630|
631|By default environment variables are split by `env_nested_delimiter` into arbitrarily deep nested fields. You can limit
632|the depth of the nested fields with the `env_nested_max_split` config setting. A common use case this is particularly useful
633|is for two-level deep settings, where the `env_nested_delimiter` (usually a single `_`) may be a substring of model
634|field names. For example:
635|
636|```bash
637|# your environment
638|export GENERATION_LLM_PROVIDER='anthropic'
639|export GENERATION_LLM_API_KEY='your-api-key'
640|export GENERATION_LLM_API_VERSION='2024-03-15'
641|```
642|
643|You could load them into the following settings model:
644|
645|```py
646|from pydantic import BaseModel
647|
648|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
649|
650|
651|class LLMConfig(BaseModel):
652|    provider: str = 'openai'
653|    api_key: str
654|    api_type: str = 'azure'
655|    api_version: str = '2023-03-15-preview'
656|
657|
658|class GenerationConfig(BaseSettings):
659|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
660|        env_nested_delimiter='_', env_nested_max_split=1, env_prefix='GENERATION_'
661|    )
662|
663|    llm: LLMConfig
664|
665|
666|print(GenerationConfig().model_dump())
667|"""
668|{
669|    'llm': {
670|        'provider': 'anthropic',
671|        'api_key': 'your-api-key',
672|        'api_type': 'azure',
673|        'api_version': '2024-03-15',
674|    }
675|}
676|"""
677|```
678|
679|Without `env_nested_max_split=1` set, `GENERATION_LLM_API_KEY` would be parsed as `llm.api.key` instead of `llm.api_key`
680|and it would raise a `ValidationError`.
681|
682|Nested environment variables take precedence over the top-level environment variable JSON
683|(e.g. in the example above, `SUB_MODEL__V2` trumps `SUB_MODEL`).
684|
685|You may also populate a complex type by providing your own source class.
686|
687|```py
688|import json
689|import os
690|from typing import Any
691|
692|from pydantic.fields import FieldInfo
693|
694|from pydantic_settings import (
695|    BaseSettings,
696|    EnvSettingsSource,
697|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
698|)
699|
700|
701|class MyCustomSource(EnvSettingsSource):
702|    def prepare_field_value(
703|        self, field_name: str, field: FieldInfo, value: Any, value_is_complex: bool
704|    ) -> Any:
705|        if field_name == 'numbers':
706|            return [int(x) for x in value.split(',')]
707|        return json.loads(value)
708|
709|
710|class Settings(BaseSettings):
711|    numbers: list[int]
712|
713|    @classmethod
714|    def settings_customise_sources(
715|        cls,
716|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
717|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
718|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
719|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
720|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
721|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
722|        return (MyCustomSource(settings_cls),)
723|
724|
725|os.environ['numbers'] = '1,2,3'
726|print(Settings().model_dump())
727|#> {'numbers': [1, 2, 3]}
728|```
729|
730|### Disabling JSON parsing
731|
732|pydantic-settings by default parses complex types from environment variables as JSON strings. This means a value
733|that is not valid JSON raises a [`SettingsError`](../api/pydantic_settings.md#pydantic_settings.SettingsError):
734|
735|```py
736|import os
737|
738|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsError
739|
740|
741|class Settings(BaseSettings):
742|    numbers: list[int]
743|
744|
745|os.environ['numbers'] = '1,2,3'
746|try:
747|    Settings()
748|except SettingsError as e:
749|    print(e)
750|    #> error parsing value for field "numbers" from source "EnvSettingsSource"
751|```
752|
753|If you want to disable this behavior for a field and parse the value in your own validator, you can annotate the
754|field with [`NoDecode`](../api/pydantic_settings.md#pydantic_settings.NoDecode):
755|
756|```py
757|import os
758|from typing import Annotated
759|
760|from pydantic import field_validator
761|
762|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, NoDecode
763|
764|
765|class Settings(BaseSettings):
766|    numbers: Annotated[list[int], NoDecode]  # (1)!
767|
768|    @field_validator('numbers', mode='before')
769|    @classmethod
770|    def decode_numbers(cls, v: str) -> list[int]:
771|        return [int(x) for x in v.split(',')]
772|
773|
774|os.environ['numbers'] = '1,2,3'
775|print(Settings().model_dump())
776|#> {'numbers': [1, 2, 3]}
777|```
778|
779|1. The `NoDecode` annotation disables JSON parsing for the `numbers` field. The `decode_numbers` field validator
780|   will be called to parse the value.
781|
782|To reuse the same parsing across multiple fields, combine `NoDecode` with a
783|[`BeforeValidator`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/validators/#annotated-validators) in a single
784|annotated type. This is a common way to accept comma-separated values, for example for CORS origins or allowed
785|hosts:
786|
787|```py
788|import os
789|from typing import Annotated, Any
790|
791|from pydantic import BeforeValidator
792|
793|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, NoDecode
794|
795|
796|def split_comma(value: Any) -> Any:
797|    if isinstance(value, str):
798|        return [item.strip() for item in value.split(',')]
799|    return value
800|
801|
802|CommaSeparated = Annotated[list[str], NoDecode, BeforeValidator(split_comma)]
803|
804|
805|class Settings(BaseSettings):
806|    cors_origins: CommaSeparated = []
807|    trusted_hosts: CommaSeparated = []
808|
809|
810|os.environ['cors_origins'] = 'https://a.com, https://b.com'
811|os.environ['trusted_hosts'] = 'a.internal'
812|print(Settings().model_dump())
813|"""
814|{'cors_origins': ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com'], 'trusted_hosts': ['a.internal']}
815|"""
816|```
817|
818|You can also disable JSON parsing for all fields by setting the `enable_decoding` config setting to `False`:
819|
820|```py
821|import os
822|
823|from pydantic import field_validator
824|
825|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
826|
827|
828|class Settings(BaseSettings):
829|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(enable_decoding=False)
830|
831|    numbers: list[int]
832|
833|    @field_validator('numbers', mode='before')
834|    @classmethod
835|    def decode_numbers(cls, v: str) -> list[int]:
836|        return [int(x) for x in v.split(',')]
837|
838|
839|os.environ['numbers'] = '1,2,3'
840|print(Settings().model_dump())
841|#> {'numbers': [1, 2, 3]}
842|```
843|
844|You can force JSON parsing for a field by annotating it with [`ForceDecode`](../api/pydantic_settings.md#pydantic_settings.ForceDecode).
845|This will bypass the `enable_decoding` config setting:
846|
847|```py
848|import os
849|from typing import Annotated
850|
851|from pydantic import field_validator
852|
853|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, ForceDecode, SettingsConfigDict
854|
855|
856|class Settings(BaseSettings):
857|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(enable_decoding=False)
858|
859|    numbers: Annotated[list[int], ForceDecode]
860|    numbers1: list[int]  # (1)!
861|
862|    @field_validator('numbers1', mode='before')
863|    @classmethod
864|    def decode_numbers1(cls, v: str) -> list[int]:
865|        return [int(x) for x in v.split(',')]
866|
867|
868|os.environ['numbers'] = '["1","2","3"]'
869|os.environ['numbers1'] = '1,2,3'
870|print(Settings().model_dump())
871|#> {'numbers': [1, 2, 3], 'numbers1': [1, 2, 3]}
872|```
873|
874|1. The `numbers1` field is not annotated with `ForceDecode`, so it will not be parsed as JSON.
875|   and we have to provide a custom validator to parse the value.
876|
877|## Nested model default partial updates
878|
879|By default, Pydantic settings does not allow partial updates to nested model default objects. This behavior can be
880|overridden by setting the `nested_model_default_partial_update` flag to `True`, which will allow partial updates on
881|nested model default object fields.
882|
883|```py
884|import os
885|
886|from pydantic import BaseModel
887|
888|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
889|
890|
891|class SubModel(BaseModel):
892|    val: int = 0
893|    flag: bool = False
894|
895|
896|class SettingsPartialUpdate(BaseSettings):
897|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
898|        env_nested_delimiter='__', nested_model_default_partial_update=True
899|    )
900|
901|    nested_model: SubModel = SubModel(val=1)
902|
903|
904|class SettingsNoPartialUpdate(BaseSettings):
905|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
906|        env_nested_delimiter='__', nested_model_default_partial_update=False
907|    )
908|
909|    nested_model: SubModel = SubModel(val=1)
910|
911|
912|# Apply a partial update to the default object using environment variables
913|os.environ['NESTED_MODEL__FLAG'] = 'True'
914|
915|# When partial update is enabled, the existing SubModel instance is updated
916|# with nested_model.flag=True change
917|assert SettingsPartialUpdate().model_dump() == {
918|    'nested_model': {'val': 1, 'flag': True}
919|}
920|
921|# When partial update is disabled, a new SubModel instance is instantiated
922|# with nested_model.flag=True change
923|assert SettingsNoPartialUpdate().model_dump() == {
924|    'nested_model': {'val': 0, 'flag': True}
925|}
926|```

928|## Dotenv (.env) support
929|
930|Dotenv files (generally named `.env`) are a common pattern that make it easy to use environment variables in a
931|platform-independent manner.
932|
933|A dotenv file follows the same general principles of all environment variables, and it looks like this:
934|
935|```bash title=".env"
936|# ignore comment
937|ENVIRONMENT="production"
938|REDIS_ADDRESS=localhost:6379
939|MEANING_OF_LIFE=42
940|MY_VAR='Hello world'
941|```
942|
943|Once you have your `.env` file filled with variables, *pydantic* supports loading it in two ways:
944|
945|1. Setting the `env_file` (and `env_file_encoding` if you don't want the default encoding of your OS) on `model_config`
946|in the `BaseSettings` class:
947|   ````py hl_lines="4 5"
948|   from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
949|
950|
951|   class Settings(BaseSettings):
952|       model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file='.env', env_file_encoding='utf-8')
953|   ````
954|2. Instantiating the `BaseSettings` derived class with the `_env_file` keyword argument
955|(and the `_env_file_encoding` if needed):
956|   ````py hl_lines="8"
957|   from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
958|
959|
960|   class Settings(BaseSettings):
961|       model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file='.env', env_file_encoding='utf-8')
962|
963|
964|   settings = Settings(_env_file='prod.env', _env_file_encoding='utf-8')
965|   ````
966|In either case, the value of the passed argument can be any valid path or filename, either absolute or relative to the
967|current working directory. From there, *pydantic* will handle everything for you by loading in your variables and
968|validating them.
969|
970|!!! note
971|    If a filename is specified for `env_file`, Pydantic will only check the current working directory and
972|    won't check any parent directories for the `.env` file. Set `env_file_depth` to the number of
973|    directory levels **up** from the current working directory that should also be checked:
974|
975|    ```py
976|    from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
977|
978|
979|    class Settings(BaseSettings):
980|        model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file='.env', env_file_depth=2)
981|    ```
982|
983|    This is only used when the file is not found in the current working directory, and only applies to
984|    relative paths. It can also be set via the `_env_file_depth` keyword argument on instantiation.
985|
986|!!! tip
987|    Named pipes (FIFOs) are also supported as dotenv files. This is useful for tools like
988|    [1Password Environments](https://developer.1password.com/docs/environments), which mount `.env` files as
989|    named pipes to provide secrets on demand without writing them to disk.
990|
991|Even when using a dotenv file, *pydantic* will still read environment variables as well as the dotenv file,
992|**environment variables will always take priority over values loaded from a dotenv file**.
993|
994|Passing a file path via the `_env_file` keyword argument on instantiation (method 2) will override
995|the value (if any) set on the `model_config` class. If the above snippets were used in conjunction, `prod.env` would be loaded
996|while `.env` would be ignored.
997|
998|If you need to load multiple dotenv files, you can pass multiple file paths as a tuple or list. The files will be
999|loaded in order, with each file overriding the previous one.
1000|
1001|```py
1002|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
1003|
1004|
1005|class Settings(BaseSettings):
1006|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
1007|        # `.env.prod` takes priority over `.env`
1008|        env_file=('.env', '.env.prod')
1009|    )
1010|```
1011|
1012|You can also use the keyword argument override to tell Pydantic not to load any file at all (even if one is set in
1013|the `model_config` class) by passing `None` as the instantiation keyword argument, e.g. `settings = Settings(_env_file=None)`.
1014|
1015|Because python-dotenv is used to parse the file, bash-like semantics such as `export` can be used which
1016|(depending on your OS and environment) may allow your dotenv file to also be used with `source`,
1017|see [python-dotenv's documentation](https://saurabh-kumar.com/python-dotenv/#usages) for more details.
1018|
1019|Pydantic settings consider `extra` config in case of dotenv file. It means if you set the `extra=forbid` (*default*)
1020|on `model_config` and your dotenv file contains an entry for a field that is not defined in settings model,
1021|it will raise `ValidationError` in settings construction.
1022|
1023|This behaviour can be customized by using the setting `dotenv_filtering` that supports two additional alternative modes:
1024|- `'match_prefix'`: only the variables that match the prefix will be passed to the model. Useful when used in conjunction with `env_prefix` to "scope" a single dotenv file to a specific model.
1025|- `'only_existing'`: only the variables that have a corresponding field will be passed to the model. When using this option the dotenv setting source will behave like the env settings source.
1026|
1027|For compatibility with pydantic 1.x BaseSettings you should use `extra=ignore`:
1028|```py
1029|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
1030|
1031|
1032|class Settings(BaseSettings):
1033|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file='.env', extra='ignore')
1034|```
1035|
1036|
1037|!!! note
1038|    Pydantic settings loads all the values from dotenv file and passes it to the model, regardless of the model's `env_prefix`, unless `dotenv_filtering` is used.
1039|    So if you provide extra values in a dotenv file, whether they start with `env_prefix` or not,
1040|    a `ValidationError` will be raised.
1041|
1042|    There is one exception to this. When `env_prefix` is set, an *unprefixed* dotenv entry whose name matches a
1043|    field name is silently skipped rather than treated as an extra value. For example, with `env_prefix='app_'`
1044|    and a `debug` field, a `debug=...` line in the dotenv file neither populates `debug` (only `app_debug` does
1045|    that) nor raises a `ValidationError` — it is simply ignored. This asymmetry can be surprising, because a
1046|    *non-matching* unprefixed entry such as `foo=...` **would** raise a `ValidationError` under the default
1047|    `extra='forbid'`.
1048|
1049|## Command Line Support
1050|
1051|Pydantic settings provides integrated CLI support, making it easy to quickly define CLI applications using Pydantic
1052|models. There are two primary use cases for Pydantic settings CLI:
1053|
1054|1. When using a CLI to override fields in Pydantic models.
1055|2. When using Pydantic models to define CLIs.
1056|
1057|By default, the experience is tailored towards use case #1 and builds on the foundations established in [parsing
1058|environment variables](#parsing-environment-variable-values). If your use case primarily falls into #2, you will likely
1059|want to enable most of the defaults outlined at the end of [creating CLI applications](#creating-cli-applications).
1060|
1061|### The Basics
1062|
1063|To get started, let's revisit the example presented in [parsing environment
1064|variables](#parsing-environment-variable-values) but using a Pydantic settings CLI:
1065|
1066|```py
1067|import sys
1068|
1069|from pydantic import BaseModel
1070|
1071|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
1072|
1073|
1074|class DeepSubModel(BaseModel):
1075|    v4: str
1076|
1077|
1078|class SubModel(BaseModel):
1079|    v1: str
1080|    v2: bytes
1081|    v3: int
1082|    deep: DeepSubModel
1083|
1084|
1085|class Settings(BaseSettings):
1086|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(cli_parse_args=True)
1087|
1088|    v0: str
1089|    sub_model: SubModel
1090|
1091|
1092|sys.argv = [
1093|    'example.py',
1094|    '--v0=0',
1095|    '--sub_model={"v1": "json-1", "v2": "json-2"}',
1096|    '--sub_model.v2=nested-2',
1097|    '--sub_model.v3=3',
1098|    '--sub_model.deep.v4=v4',
1099|]
1100|
1101|print(Settings().model_dump())
1102|"""
1103|{
1104|    'v0': '0',
1105|    'sub_model': {'v1': 'json-1', 'v2': b'nested-2', 'v3': 3, 'deep': {'v4': 'v4'}},
1106|}
1107|"""
1108|```
1109|
1110|To enable CLI parsing, we simply set the `cli_parse_args` flag to a valid value, which retains similar connotations as
1111|defined in `argparse`.
1112|
1113|Note that a CLI settings source is [**the topmost source**](#field-value-priority) by default unless its [priority value
1114|is customised](#customise-settings-sources):
1115|
1116|```py
1117|import os
1118|import sys
1119|
1120|from pydantic_settings import (
1121|    BaseSettings,
1122|    CliSettingsSource,
1123|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
1124|)
1125|
1126|
1127|class Settings(BaseSettings):
1128|    my_foo: str
1129|
1130|    @classmethod
1131|    def settings_customise_sources(
1132|        cls,
1133|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
1134|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
1135|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
1136|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
1137|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
1138|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
1139|        return env_settings, CliSettingsSource(settings_cls, cli_parse_args=True)
1140|
1141|
1142|os.environ['MY_FOO'] = 'from environment'
1143|
1144|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_foo=from cli']
1145|
1146|print(Settings().model_dump())
1147|#> {'my_foo': 'from environment'}
1148|```
1149|
1150|#### Lists
1151|
1152|CLI argument parsing of lists supports intermixing of any of the below three styles:
1153|
1154|  * JSON style `--field='[1,2]'`
1155|  * Argparse style `--field 1 --field 2`
1156|  * Lazy style `--field=1,2`
1157|
1158|Use the JSON style `--field='[]'` to pass an empty list. Empty arrays contribute no items when mixed with other list arguments.
1159|
1160|```py
1161|import sys
1162|
1163|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
1164|
1165|
1166|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True):
1167|    my_list: list[int]
1168|
1169|
1170|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_list', '[1,2]']
1171|print(Settings().model_dump())
1172|#> {'my_list': [1, 2]}
1173|
1174|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_list', '1', '--my_list', '2']
1175|print(Settings().model_dump())
1176|#> {'my_list': [1, 2]}
1177|
1178|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_list', '1,2']
1179|print(Settings().model_dump())
1180|#> {'my_list': [1, 2]}
1181|
1182|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_list', '[]']
1183|print(Settings().model_dump())
1184|#> {'my_list': []}
1185|
1186|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_list', '[]', '--my_list', '3']
1187|print(Settings().model_dump())
1188|#> {'my_list': [3]}
1189|```
1190|
1191|#### Dictionaries
1192|
1193|CLI argument parsing of dictionaries supports intermixing of any of the below two styles:
1194|
1195|  * JSON style `--field='{"k1": 1, "k2": 2}'`
1196|  * Environment variable style `--field k1=1 --field k2=2`
1197|
1198|These can be used in conjunction with list forms as well, e.g:
1199|
1200|  * `--field k1=1,k2=2 --field k3=3 --field '{"k4": 4}'` etc.
1201|
1202|```py
1203|import sys
1204|
1205|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
1206|
1207|
1208|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True):
1209|    my_dict: dict[str, int]
1210|
1211|
1212|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_dict', '{"k1":1,"k2":2}']
1213|print(Settings().model_dump())
1214|#> {'my_dict': {'k1': 1, 'k2': 2}}
1215|
1216|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--my_dict', 'k1=1', '--my_dict', 'k2=2']
1217|print(Settings().model_dump())
1218|#> {'my_dict': {'k1': 1, 'k2': 2}}
1219|```
1220|
1221|#### Literals and Enums
1222|
1223|CLI argument parsing of literals and enums are converted into CLI choices.
1224|
1225|```py
1226|import sys
1227|from enum import IntEnum
1228|from typing import Literal
1229|
1230|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
1231|
1232|
1233|class Fruit(IntEnum):
1234|    pear = 0
1235|    kiwi = 1
1236|    lime = 2
1237|
1238|
1239|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True):
1240|    fruit: Fruit
1241|    pet: Literal['dog', 'cat', 'bird']
1242|
1243|
1244|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--fruit', 'lime', '--pet', 'cat']
1245|print(Settings().model_dump())
1246|#> {'fruit': <Fruit.lime: 2>, 'pet': 'cat'}
1247|```
1248|
1249|#### Aliases
1250|
1251|Pydantic field aliases are added as CLI argument aliases. Aliases of length one are converted into short options.
1252|
1253|```py
1254|import sys
1255|
1256|from pydantic import AliasChoices, AliasPath, Field
1257|
1258|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
1259|
1260|
1261|class User(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True):
1262|    first_name: str = Field(
1263|        validation_alias=AliasChoices('f', 'fname', AliasPath('fullname', 0))
1264|    )
1265|    last_name: str = Field(
1266|        validation_alias=AliasChoices('l', 'lname', AliasPath('fullname', 1))
1267|    )
1268|
1269|
1270|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--fname', 'John', '--lname', 'Doe']
1271|print(User().model_dump())
1272|#> {'first_name': 'John', 'last_name': 'Doe'}
1273|
1274|sys.argv = ['example.py', '-f', 'John', '-l', 'Doe']
1275|print(User().model_dump())
1276|#> {'first_name': 'John', 'last_name': 'Doe'}
1277|
1278|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--fullname', 'John,Doe']
1279|print(User().model_dump())
1280|#> {'first_name': 'John', 'last_name': 'Doe'}
1281|
1282|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--fullname', 'John', '--lname', 'Doe']
1283|print(User().model_dump())
1284|#> {'first_name': 'John', 'last_name': 'Doe'}
1285|```
1286|
1287|### Variadic named options
1288|
1289|Collection fields are repeated options by default (`--param a --param b`). This covers any
1290|`Sequence`, `Set`, or `Mapping` type, including subclasses such as `tuple`, `frozenset`,
1291|`deque`, and `OrderedDict`. `str`, `bytes`, and `bytearray` are sequences too, but they take
1292|a single value. Wrap a collection field in `CliVariadicArg` to accept remaining values after
1293|a single option (`--param a b c`).
1294|
1295|Repeating the option **replaces** the previous values (`--param a b --param c` becomes
1296|`['c']`), which is the opposite of `action=append`. `nargs='*'` is greedy: it consumes
1297|values until the next option flag, so a following subcommand name can be swallowed.
1298|
1299|`CliVariadicArg` is ignored on `AliasPath` fields; those still use `action=append`.
1300|
1301|### Subcommands and Positional Arguments
1302|
1303|Subcommands and positional arguments are expressed using the `CliSubCommand` and `CliPositionalArg` annotations. The
1304|subcommand annotation can only be applied to required fields (i.e. fields that do not have a default value).
1305|Furthermore, subcommands must be a valid type derived from either a pydantic `BaseModel` or pydantic.dataclasses
1306|`dataclass`.
1307|
1308|Parsed subcommands can be retrieved from model instances using the `get_subcommand` utility function. If a subcommand is
1309|not required, set the `is_required` flag to `False` to disable raising an error if no subcommand is found.
1310|
1311|!!! note
1312|    CLI settings subcommands are limited to a single subparser per model. In other words, all subcommands for a model
1313|    are grouped under a single subparser; it does not allow for multiple subparsers with each subparser having its own
1314|    set of subcommands. For more information on subparsers, see [argparse
1315|    subcommands](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html#sub-commands).
1316|
1317|!!! note
1318|    `CliSubCommand` and `CliPositionalArg` are always case sensitive.
1319|
1320|```py
1321|import sys
1322|
1323|from pydantic import BaseModel
1324|
1325|from pydantic_settings import (
1326|    BaseSettings,
1327|    CliPositionalArg,
1328|    CliSubCommand,
1329|    SettingsError,
1330|    get_subcommand,
1331|)
1332|
1333|
1334|class Init(BaseModel):
1335|    directory: CliPositionalArg[str]
1336|
1337|
1338|class Clone(BaseModel):
1339|    repository: CliPositionalArg[str]
1340|    directory: CliPositionalArg[str]
1341|
1342|
1343|class Git(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_exit_on_error=False):
1344|    clone: CliSubCommand[Clone]
1345|    init: CliSubCommand[Init]
1346|
1347|
1348|# Run without subcommands
1349|sys.argv = ['example.py']
1350|cmd = Git()
1351|assert cmd.model_dump() == {'clone': None, 'init': None}
1352|
1353|try:
1354|    # Will raise an error since no subcommand was provided
1355|    get_subcommand(cmd).model_dump()
1356|except SettingsError as err:
1357|    assert str(err) == 'Error: CLI subcommand is required {clone, init}'
1358|
1359|# Will not raise an error since subcommand is not required
1360|assert get_subcommand(cmd, is_required=False) is None
1361|
1362|
1363|# Run the clone subcommand
1364|sys.argv = ['example.py', 'clone', 'repo', 'dest']
1365|cmd = Git()
1366|assert cmd.model_dump() == {
1367|    'clone': {'repository': 'repo', 'directory': 'dest'},
1368|    'init': None,
1369|}
1370|
1371|# Returns the subcommand model instance (in this case, 'clone')
1372|assert get_subcommand(cmd).model_dump() == {
1373|    'directory': 'dest',
1374|    'repository': 'repo',
1375|}
1376|```
1377|
1378|The `CliSubCommand` and `CliPositionalArg` annotations also support union operations and aliases. For unions of Pydantic
1379|models, it is important to remember the [nuances](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/unions/) that can arise
1380|during validation. Specifically, for unions of subcommands that are identical in content, it is recommended to break
1381|them out into separate `CliSubCommand` fields to avoid any complications. Lastly, the derived subcommand names from
1382|unions will be the names of the Pydantic model classes themselves.
1383|
1384|When assigning aliases to `CliSubCommand` or `CliPositionalArg` fields, only a single alias can be assigned. For
1385|non-union subcommands, aliasing will change the displayed help text and subcommand name. Conversely, for union
1386|subcommands, aliasing will have no tangible effect from the perspective of the CLI settings source. Lastly, for
1387|positional arguments, aliasing will change the CLI help text displayed for the field.
1388|
1389|```py
1390|import sys
1391|from typing import Union
1392|
1393|from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
1394|
1395|from pydantic_settings import (
1396|    BaseSettings,
1397|    CliPositionalArg,
1398|    CliSubCommand,
1399|    get_subcommand,
1400|)
1401|
1402|
1403|class Alpha(BaseModel):
1404|    """Apha Help"""
1405|
1406|    cmd_alpha: CliPositionalArg[str] = Field(alias='alpha-cmd')
1407|
1408|
1409|class Beta(BaseModel):
1410|    """Beta Help"""
1411|
1412|    opt_beta: str = Field(alias='opt-beta')
1413|
1414|
1415|class Gamma(BaseModel):
1416|    """Gamma Help"""
1417|
1418|    opt_gamma: str = Field(alias='opt-gamma')
1419|
1420|
1421|class Root(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_exit_on_error=False):
1422|    alpha_or_beta: CliSubCommand[Union[Alpha, Beta]] = Field(alias='alpha-or-beta-cmd')
1423|    gamma: CliSubCommand[Gamma] = Field(alias='gamma-cmd')
1424|
1425|
1426|sys.argv = ['example.py', 'Alpha', 'hello']
1427|assert get_subcommand(Root()).model_dump() == {'cmd_alpha': 'hello'}
1428|
1429|sys.argv = ['example.py', 'Beta', '--opt-beta=hey']
1430|assert get_subcommand(Root()).model_dump() == {'opt_beta': 'hey'}
1431|
1432|sys.argv = ['example.py', 'gamma-cmd', '--opt-gamma=hi']
1433|assert get_subcommand(Root()).model_dump() == {'opt_gamma': 'hi'}
1434|```
1435|
1436|### Creating CLI Applications
1437|
1438|The `CliApp` class provides two utility methods, `CliApp.run` and `CliApp.run_subcommand`, that can be used to run a
1439|Pydantic `BaseSettings`, `BaseModel`, or `pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass` as a CLI application. Primarily, the methods
1440|provide structure for running `cli_cmd` methods associated with models.
1441|
1442|`CliApp.run` can be used in directly providing the `cli_args` to be parsed, and will run the model `cli_cmd` method (if
1443|defined) after instantiation:
1444|
1445|```py
1446|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliApp
1447|
1448|
1449|class Settings(BaseSettings):
1450|    this_foo: str
1451|
1452|    def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1453|        # Print the parsed data
1454|        print(self.model_dump())
1455|        #> {'this_foo': 'is such a foo'}
1456|
1457|        # Update the parsed data showing cli_cmd ran
1458|        self.this_foo = 'ran the foo cli cmd'
1459|
1460|
1461|s = CliApp.run(Settings, cli_args=['--this_foo', 'is such a foo'])
1462|print(s.model_dump())
1463|#> {'this_foo': 'ran the foo cli cmd'}
1464|```
1465|
1466|Similarly, the `CliApp.run_subcommand` can be used in recursive fashion to run the `cli_cmd` method of a subcommand:
1467|
1468|```py
1469|from pydantic import BaseModel
1470|
1471|from pydantic_settings import CliApp, CliPositionalArg, CliSubCommand
1472|
1473|
1474|class Init(BaseModel):
1475|    directory: CliPositionalArg[str]
1476|
1477|    def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1478|        print(f'git init "{self.directory}"')
1479|        #> git init "dir"
1480|        self.directory = 'ran the git init cli cmd'
1481|
1482|
1483|class Clone(BaseModel):
1484|    repository: CliPositionalArg[str]
1485|    directory: CliPositionalArg[str]
1486|
1487|    def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1488|        print(f'git clone from "{self.repository}" into "{self.directory}"')
1489|        self.directory = 'ran the clone cli cmd'
1490|
1491|
1492|class Git(BaseModel):
1493|    clone: CliSubCommand[Clone]
1494|    init: CliSubCommand[Init]
1495|
1496|    def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1497|        CliApp.run_subcommand(self)
1498|
1499|
1500|cmd = CliApp.run(Git, cli_args=['init', 'dir'])
1501|assert cmd.model_dump() == {
1502|    'clone': None,
1503|    'init': {'directory': 'ran the git init cli cmd'},
1504|}
1505|```
1506|
1507|!!! note
1508|    Unlike `CliApp.run`, `CliApp.run_subcommand` requires the subcommand model to have a defined `cli_cmd` method.
1509|
1510|For `BaseModel` and `pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass` types, `CliApp.run` will internally use the following
1511|`BaseSettings` configuration defaults:
1512|
1513|* `nested_model_default_partial_update=True`
1514|* `case_sensitive=True`
1515|* `cli_hide_none_type=True`
1516|* `cli_avoid_json=True`
1517|* `cli_enforce_required=True`
1518|* `cli_implicit_flags=True`
1519|* `cli_kebab_case=True`
1520|
1521|#### Asynchronous Commands
1522|
1523|Pydantic settings supports running asynchronous CLI commands via `CliApp.run` and `CliApp.run_subcommand`. With this feature, you can define async def methods within your Pydantic models (including subcommands) and have them executed just like their synchronous counterparts. Specifically:
1524|
1525|1. Asynchronous methods are supported: You can now mark your cli_cmd or similar CLI entrypoint methods as async def and have CliApp execute them.
1526|2. Subcommands may also be asynchronous: If you have nested CLI subcommands, the final (lowest-level) subcommand methods can likewise be asynchronous.
1527|3. Limit asynchronous methods to final subcommands: Defining parent commands as asynchronous is not recommended, because it can result in additional threads and event loops being created. For best performance and to avoid unnecessary resource usage, only implement your deepest (child) subcommands as async def.
1528|
1529|Below is a simple example demonstrating an asynchronous top-level command:
1530|
1531|```py
1532|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliApp
1533|
1534|
1535|class AsyncSettings(BaseSettings):
1536|    async def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1537|        print('Hello from an async CLI method!')
1538|        #> Hello from an async CLI method!
1539|
1540|
1541|# If an event loop is already running, a new thread will be used;
1542|# otherwise, asyncio.run() is used to execute this async method.
1543|assert CliApp.run(AsyncSettings, cli_args=[]).model_dump() == {}
1544|```
1545|
1546|#### Asynchronous Subcommands
1547|
1548|As mentioned above, you can also define subcommands as async. However, only do so for the leaf (lowest-level) subcommand to avoid spawning new threads and event loops unnecessarily in parent commands:
1549|
1550|```py
1551|from pydantic import BaseModel
1552|
1553|from pydantic_settings import (
1554|    BaseSettings,
1555|    CliApp,
1556|    CliPositionalArg,
1557|    CliSubCommand,
1558|)
1559|
1560|
1561|class Clone(BaseModel):
1562|    repository: CliPositionalArg[str]
1563|    directory: CliPositionalArg[str]
1564|
1565|    async def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1566|        # Perform async tasks here, e.g. network or I/O operations
1567|        print(f'Cloning async from "{self.repository}" into "{self.directory}"')
1568|        #> Cloning async from "repo" into "dir"
1569|
1570|
1571|class Git(BaseSettings):
1572|    clone: CliSubCommand[Clone]
1573|
1574|    def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1575|        # Run the final subcommand (clone/init). It is recommended to define async methods only at the deepest level.
1576|        CliApp.run_subcommand(self)
1577|
1578|
1579|assert CliApp.run(Git, cli_args=['clone', 'repo', 'dir']).model_dump() == {
1580|    'clone': {'repository': 'repo', 'directory': 'dir'}
1581|}
1582|```
1583|
1584|When executing a subcommand with an asynchronous cli_cmd, Pydantic settings automatically detects whether the current thread already has an active event loop. If so, the async command is run in a fresh thread to avoid conflicts. Otherwise, it uses asyncio.run() in the current thread. This handling ensures your asynchronous subcommands "just work" without additional manual setup.
1585|
1586|#### Printing Help
1587|
1588|The `print_help` and `format_help` methods are available for printing or formatting help.
1589|
1590|```python
1591|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliApp
1592|
1593|
1594|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_prog_name='example'):
1595|
1596|    def cli_cmd(self) -> None:
1597|        # Will print help for the current command or subcommand instance.
1598|        CliApp.print_help(self)
1599|
1600|        # Will return formatted help for the current command or subcommand instance.
1601|        CliApp.format_help(self)
1602|
1603|
1604|CliApp.run(Settings, cli_args=[])
1605|"""
1606|usage: example [-h]
1607|
1608|options:
1609|  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
1610|"""
1611|
1612|# You can also print or format help on the class itself.
1613|print(CliApp.format_help(Settings))
1614|"""
1615|usage: example [-h]
1616|
1617|options:
1618|  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
1619|"""
1620|```
1621|
1622|#### Serializing Arguments
1623|
1624|An instantiated Pydantic model can be serialized into its CLI arguments using the `CliApp.serialize` method. Serialization styles can be controlled using the `list_style`, `dict_style`, and `positionals_first` flags.
1625|
1626|```py
1627|from pydantic import BaseModel
1628|
1629|from pydantic_settings import CliApp, CliPositionalArg
1630|
1631|
1632|class Nested(BaseModel):
1633|    that: dict[str, int]
1634|
1635|
1636|class Settings(BaseModel):
1637|    positional_arg: CliPositionalArg[str]
1638|    this: list[str]
1639|    nested: Nested
1640|
1641|
1642|settings = Settings(
1643|    positional_arg='arg', this=['hello', 'world'], nested=Nested(that={'a': 1, 'b': 2})
1644|)
1645|
1646|print(CliApp.serialize(settings))
1647|#> ['--this', '["hello", "world"]', '--nested.that', '{"a": 1, "b": 2}', 'arg']
1648|
1649|print(CliApp.serialize(settings, positionals_first=True))
1650|#> ['arg', '--this', '["hello", "world"]', '--nested.that', '{"a": 1, "b": 2}']
1651|
1652|print(CliApp.serialize(settings, list_style='lazy'))
1653|#> ['--this', 'hello,world', '--nested.that', '{"a": 1, "b": 2}', 'arg']
1654|
1655|print(CliApp.serialize(settings, list_style='argparse'))
1656|#> ['--this', 'hello', '--this', 'world', '--nested.that', '{"a": 1, "b": 2}', 'arg']
1657|
1658|print(CliApp.serialize(settings, dict_style='env'))
1659|"""
1660|['--this', '["hello", "world"]', '--nested.that', 'a=1', '--nested.that', 'b=2', 'arg']
1661|"""
1662|```
1663|
1664|### Mutually Exclusive Groups
1665|
1666|CLI mutually exclusive groups can be created by inheriting from the `CliMutuallyExclusiveGroup` class.
1667|
1668|!!! note
1669|    A `CliMutuallyExclusiveGroup` cannot be used in a union or contain nested models.
1670|
1671|```py
1672|from typing import Optional
1673|
1674|from pydantic import BaseModel
1675|
1676|from pydantic_settings import CliApp, CliMutuallyExclusiveGroup, SettingsError
1677|
1678|
1679|class Circle(CliMutuallyExclusiveGroup):
1680|    radius: Optional[float] = None
1681|    diameter: Optional[float] = None
1682|    perimeter: Optional[float] = None
1683|
1684|
1685|class Settings(BaseModel):
1686|    circle: Circle
1687|
1688|
1689|try:
1690|    CliApp.run(
1691|        Settings,
1692|        cli_args=['--circle.radius=1', '--circle.diameter=2'],
1693|        cli_exit_on_error=False,
1694|    )
1695|except SettingsError as e:
1696|    print(e)
1697|    """
1698|    error parsing CLI: argument --circle.diameter: not allowed with argument --circle.radius
1699|    """
1700|```
1701|
1702|### Customizing the CLI Experience
1703|
1704|The below flags can be used to customise the CLI experience to your needs.
1705|
1706|#### Change the Displayed Program Name
1707|
1708|Change the default program name displayed in the help text usage by setting `cli_prog_name`. By default, it will derive
1709|the name of the currently executing program from `sys.argv[0]`, just like argparse.
1710|
1711|```py
1712|import sys
1713|
1714|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
1715|
1716|
1717|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_prog_name='appdantic'):
1718|    pass
1719|
1720|
1721|try:
1722|    sys.argv = ['example.py', '--help']
1723|    Settings()
1724|except SystemExit as e:
1725|    print(e)
1726|    #> 0
1727|"""
1728|usage: appdantic [-h]
1729|
1730|options:
1731|  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
1732|"""
1733|```
1734|
1735|#### CLI Boolean Flags
1736|
1737|Change whether boolean fields should be explicit or implicit by default using the `cli_implicit_flags` setting. By
1738|default, boolean fields are "explicit", meaning a boolean value must be explicitly provided on the CLI, e.g.
1739|`--flag=True`. Conversely, boolean fields that are "implicit" derive the value from the flag itself, e.g.
1740|`--flag,--no-flag`, which removes the need for an explicit value to be passed.
1741|
1742|Additionally, the provided `CliImplicitFlag` and `CliExplicitFlag` annotations can be used for more granular control
1743|when necessary.
1744|
1745|```py
1746|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliExplicitFlag, CliImplicitFlag
1747|
1748|
1749|class ExplicitSettings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True):
1750|    """Boolean fields are explicit by default."""
1751|
1752|    explicit_req: bool
1753|    """
1754|    --explicit_req bool   (required)
1755|    """
1756|
1757|    explicit_opt: bool = False
1758|    """
1759|    --explicit_opt bool   (default: False)
1760|    """
1761|
1762|    # Booleans are explicit by default, so must override implicit flags with annotation
1763|    implicit_req: CliImplicitFlag[bool]
1764|    """
1765|    --implicit_req, --no-implicit_req (required)
1766|    """
1767|
1768|    implicit_opt: CliImplicitFlag[bool] = False
1769|    """
1770|    --implicit_opt, --no-implicit_opt (default: False)
1771|    """
1772|
1773|
1774|class ImplicitSettings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_implicit_flags=True):
1775|    """With cli_implicit_flags=True, boolean fields are implicit by default."""
1776|
1777|    # Booleans are implicit by default, so must override explicit flags with annotation
1778|    explicit_req: CliExplicitFlag[bool]
1779|    """
1780|    --explicit_req bool   (required)
1781|    """
1782|
1783|    explicit_opt: CliExplicitFlag[bool] = False
1784|    """
1785|    --explicit_opt bool   (default: False)
1786|    """
1787|
1788|    implicit_req: bool
1789|    """
1790|    --implicit_req, --no-implicit_req (required)
1791|    """
1792|
1793|    implicit_opt: bool = False
1794|    """
1795|    --implicit_opt, --no-implicit_opt (default: False)
1796|    """
1797|```
1798|
1799|Implicit flag behavior can be further refined using the "toggle" or "dual" mode settings. Similarly, the provided
1800|`CliToggleFlag` and `CliDualFlag` annotations can be used for more granular control.
1801|
1802|For "toggle" flags, if default=`False`, `--flag` will store `True`. Otherwise, if default=`True`, `--no-flag` will store
1803|`False`.
1804|
1805|```py
1806|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliDualFlag, CliToggleFlag
1807|
1808|
1809|class ImplicitDualSettings(
1810|    BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_implicit_flags='dual'
1811|):
1812|    """With cli_implicit_flags='dual', implicit flags are dual by default."""
1813|
1814|    implicit_req: bool
1815|    """
1816|    --implicit_req, --no-implicit_req (required)
1817|    """
1818|
1819|    implicit_dual_opt: bool = False
1820|    """
1821|    --implicit_dual_opt, --no-implicit_dual_opt (default: False)
1822|    """
1823|
1824|    # Implicit flags are dual by default, so must override toggle flags with annotation
1825|    flag_a: CliToggleFlag[bool] = False
1826|    """
1827|    --flag_a (default: False)
1828|    """
1829|
1830|    # Implicit flags are dual by default, so must override toggle flags with annotation
1831|    flag_b: CliToggleFlag[bool] = True
1832|    """
1833|    --no-flag_b (default: True)
1834|    """
1835|
1836|
1837|class ImplicitToggleSettings(
1838|    BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_implicit_flags='toggle'
1839|):
1840|    """With cli_implicit_flags='toggle', implicit flags are toggle by default."""
1841|
1842|    implicit_req: bool
1843|    """
1844|    --implicit_req, --no-implicit_req (required)
1845|    """
1846|
1847|    # Implicit flags are toggle by default, so must override dual flags with annotation
1848|    implicit_dual_opt: CliDualFlag[bool] = False
1849|    """
1850|    --implicit_dual_opt, --no-implicit_dual_opt (default: False)
1851|    """
1852|
1853|    flag_a: bool = False
1854|    """
1855|    --flag_a (default: False)
1856|    """
1857|
1858|    flag_b: bool = True
1859|    """
1860|    --no-flag_b (default: True)
1861|    """
1862|```
1863|
1864|#### Ignore and Retrieve Unknown Arguments
1865|
1866|Change whether to ignore unknown CLI arguments and only parse known ones using `cli_ignore_unknown_args`. By default, the CLI
1867|does not ignore any args. Ignored arguments can then be retrieved using the `CliUnknownArgs` annotation.
1868|
1869|```py
1870|import sys
1871|
1872|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliUnknownArgs
1873|
1874|
1875|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_ignore_unknown_args=True):
1876|    good_arg: str
1877|    ignored_args: CliUnknownArgs
1878|
1879|
1880|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--bad-arg=bad', 'ANOTHER_BAD_ARG', '--good_arg=hello world']
1881|print(Settings().model_dump())
1882|#> {'good_arg': 'hello world', 'ignored_args': ['--bad-arg=bad', 'ANOTHER_BAD_ARG']}
1883|```
1884|
1885|With subcommands, unknown arguments are captured by the innermost parser that declares a `CliUnknownArgs` field.
1886|Arguments appearing before a subcommand remain with the parent parser. If a child parser has no capture field,
1887|its leftovers are passed back to its parent. Captured lists are reset when a `CliSettingsSource` parses new arguments.
1888|
1889|Ordinary nested models share their parent's parser. Declaring multiple `CliUnknownArgs` fields on that same parser
1890|still duplicates its leftovers; this case is not covered by the subcommand behavior above. Custom parsers whose
1891|`parse_known_args` method cannot be replaced also cannot capture subcommand leftovers independently.
1892|
1893|#### CLI Kebab Case for Arguments
1894|
1895|Change whether CLI arguments should use kebab case by enabling `cli_kebab_case`. By default, `cli_kebab_case=True` will
1896|ignore enum fields, and is equivalent to `cli_kebab_case='no_enums'`. To apply kebab case to everything, including
1897|enums, use `cli_kebab_case='all'`.
1898|
1899|```py
1900|import sys
1901|
1902|from pydantic import Field
1903|
1904|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
1905|
1906|
1907|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_kebab_case=True):
1908|    my_option: str = Field(description='will show as kebab case on CLI')
1909|
1910|
1911|try:
1912|    sys.argv = ['example.py', '--help']
1913|    Settings()
1914|except SystemExit as e:
1915|    print(e)
1916|    #> 0
1917|"""
1918|usage: example.py [-h] [--my-option str]
1919|
1920|options:
1921|  -h, --help       show this help message and exit
1922|  --my-option str  will show as kebab case on CLI (required)
1923|"""
1924|```
1925|
1926|#### Change Whether CLI Should Exit on Error
1927|
1928|Change whether the CLI internal parser will exit on error or raise a `SettingsError` exception by using
1929|`cli_exit_on_error`. By default, the CLI internal parser will exit on error.
1930|
1931|```py
1932|import sys
1933|
1934|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsError
1935|
1936|
1937|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_exit_on_error=False): ...
1938|
1939|
1940|try:
1941|    sys.argv = ['example.py', '--bad-arg']
1942|    Settings()
1943|except SettingsError as e:
1944|    print(e)
1945|    #> error parsing CLI: unrecognized arguments: --bad-arg
1946|```
1947|
1948|#### Enforce Required Arguments at CLI
1949|
1950|Pydantic settings is designed to pull values in from various sources when instantiating a model. This means a field that
1951|is required is not strictly required from any single source (e.g. the CLI). Instead, all that matters is that one of the
1952|sources provides the required value.
1953|
1954|However, if your use case [aligns more with #2](#command-line-support), using Pydantic models to define CLIs, you will
1955|likely want required fields to be _strictly required at the CLI_. We can enable this behavior by using
1956|`cli_enforce_required`.
1957|
1958|!!! note
1959|    A required `CliPositionalArg` field is always strictly required (enforced) at the CLI.
1960|
1961|```py
1962|import os
1963|import sys
1964|
1965|from pydantic import Field
1966|
1967|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsError
1968|
1969|
1970|class Settings(
1971|    BaseSettings,
1972|    cli_parse_args=True,
1973|    cli_enforce_required=True,
1974|    cli_exit_on_error=False,
1975|):
1976|    my_required_field: str = Field(description='a top level required field')
1977|
1978|
1979|os.environ['MY_REQUIRED_FIELD'] = 'hello from environment'
1980|
1981|try:
1982|    sys.argv = ['example.py']
1983|    Settings()
1984|except SettingsError as e:
1985|    print(e)
1986|    #> error parsing CLI: the following arguments are required: --my_required_field
1987|```
1988|
1989|#### Change the None Type Parse String
1990|
1991|Change the CLI string value that will be parsed (e.g. "null", "void", "None", etc.) into `None` by setting
1992|`cli_parse_none_str`. By default it will use the `env_parse_none_str` value if set. Otherwise, it will default to "null"
1993|if `cli_avoid_json` is `False`, and "None" if `cli_avoid_json` is `True`.
1994|
1995|```py
1996|import sys
1997|from typing import Optional
1998|
1999|from pydantic import Field
2000|
2001|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
2002|
2003|
2004|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_parse_none_str='void'):
2005|    v1: Optional[int] = Field(description='the top level v0 option')
2006|
2007|
2008|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--v1', 'void']
2009|print(Settings().model_dump())
2010|#> {'v1': None}
2011|```
2012|
2013|#### Hide None Type Values
2014|
2015|Hide `None` values from the CLI help text by enabling `cli_hide_none_type`.
2016|
2017|```py
2018|import sys
2019|from typing import Optional
2020|
2021|from pydantic import Field
2022|
2023|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
2024|
2025|
2026|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_hide_none_type=True):
2027|    v0: Optional[str] = Field(description='the top level v0 option')
2028|
2029|
2030|try:
2031|    sys.argv = ['example.py', '--help']
2032|    Settings()
2033|except SystemExit as e:
2034|    print(e)
2035|    #> 0
2036|"""
2037|usage: example.py [-h] [--v0 str]
2038|
2039|options:
2040|  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
2041|  --v0 str    the top level v0 option (required)
2042|"""
2043|```
2044|
2045|#### Avoid Adding JSON CLI Options
2046|
2047|Avoid adding complex fields that result in JSON strings at the CLI by enabling `cli_avoid_json`.
2048|
2049|```py
2050|import sys
2051|
2052|from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
2053|
2054|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
2055|
2056|
2057|class SubModel(BaseModel):
2058|    v1: int = Field(description='the sub model v1 option')
2059|
2060|
2061|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_avoid_json=True):
2062|    sub_model: SubModel = Field(
2063|        description='The help summary for SubModel related options'
2064|    )
2065|
2066|
2067|try:
2068|    sys.argv = ['example.py', '--help']
2069|    Settings()
2070|except SystemExit as e:
2071|    print(e)
2072|    #> 0
2073|"""
2074|usage: example.py [-h] [--sub_model.v1 int]
2075|
2076|options:
2077|  -h, --help          show this help message and exit
2078|
2079|sub_model options:
2080|  The help summary for SubModel related options
2081|
2082|  --sub_model.v1 int  the sub model v1 option (required)
2083|"""

2086|#### Use Class Docstring for Group Help Text
2087|
2088|By default, when populating the group help text for nested models it will pull from the field descriptions.
2089|Alternatively, we can also configure CLI settings to pull from the class docstring instead.
2090|
2091|!!! note
2092|    If the field is a union of nested models the group help text will always be pulled from the field description;
2093|    even if `cli_use_class_docs_for_groups` is set to `True`.
2094|
2095|```py
2096|import sys
2097|
2098|from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
2099|
2100|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
2101|
2102|
2103|class SubModel(BaseModel):
2104|    """The help text from the class docstring."""
2105|
2106|    v1: int = Field(description='the sub model v1 option')
2107|
2108|
2109|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_use_class_docs_for_groups=True):
2110|    """My application help text."""
2111|
2112|    sub_model: SubModel = Field(description='The help text from the field description')
2113|
2114|
2115|try:
2116|    sys.argv = ['example.py', '--help']
2117|    Settings()
2118|except SystemExit as e:
2119|    print(e)
2120|    #> 0
2121|"""
2122|usage: example.py [-h] [--sub_model JSON] [--sub_model.v1 int]
2123|
2124|My application help text.
2125|
2126|options:
2127|  -h, --help          show this help message and exit
2128|
2129|sub_model options:
2130|  The help text from the class docstring.
2131|
2132|  --sub_model JSON    set sub_model from JSON string
2133|  --sub_model.v1 int  the sub model v1 option (required)
2134|"""
2135|```

2137|#### Show Environment Variables in CLI Help
2138|
2139|Enable `cli_show_env_vars` to append the resolved environment variable name for each CLI option in help text. This is
2140|useful for ops runbooks, configuration discovery, and 12-factor apps where the same settings can be provided either by
2141|CLI flags or environment variables.
2142|
2143|```py
2144|from pydantic import Field
2145|
2146|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliApp, SettingsConfigDict
2147|
2148|
2149|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2150|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
2151|        cli_parse_args=True,
2152|        cli_show_env_vars=True,
2153|        cli_prog_name='example.py',
2154|        env_prefix='MYAPP_',
2155|    )
2156|
2157|    redis_host: str = Field(description='Redis hostname')
2158|
2159|
2160|print(CliApp.format_help(Settings))
2161|"""
2162|usage: example.py [-h] [--redis_host str]
2163|
2164|options:
2165|  -h, --help        show this help message and exit
2166|  --redis_host str  Redis hostname (required) [env: MYAPP_REDIS_HOST]
2167|"""
2168|```
2169|
2170|When a field uses `AliasChoices`, all resolved environment variable names are rendered in order, for example
2171|`[env: API_KEY | LEGACY_API_KEY]`. If you construct a `CliSettingsSource` directly with `cli_show_env_vars=True`, the
2172|same names are also available as a simple `env_var_names` mapping keyed by CLI destination.
2173|
2174|When `CliSettingsSource` is constructed directly without passing `_env_settings_source`, a fallback
2175|`EnvSettingsSource(settings_cls)` is used for help text resolution. This reflects model config values, but does not
2176|include source-level constructor overrides (for example, custom `env_prefix` or `env_nested_delimiter`) unless you
2177|pass that customized source explicitly.
2178|
2179|#### Change the CLI Flag Prefix Character

2184|import sys

2187|

2191|class Settings(BaseSettings, cli_parse_args=True, cli_flag_prefix_char='+'):

2200|print(Settings().model_dump())
