2240|#### CLI Shortcuts for Arguments
2241|
2242|Add alternative CLI argument names (shortcuts) for fields using the `cli_shortcuts` option in `SettingsConfigDict`. This allows you to define additional names for CLI arguments, which can be especially useful for providing more user-friendly or shorter aliases for deeply nested or verbose field names.
2243|
2244|The `cli_shortcuts` option takes a dictionary mapping the target field name (using dot notation for nested fields) to one or more shortcut names. If multiple fields share the same shortcut, the first matching field will take precedence.
2245|
2246|**Flat Example:**
2247|
2248|```py
2249|from pydantic import Field
2250|
2251|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
2252|
2253|
2254|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2255|    option: str = Field(default='foo')
2256|    list_option: str = Field(default='fizz')
2257|
2258|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
2259|        cli_shortcuts={'option': 'option2', 'list_option': ['list_option2']}
2260|    )
2261|
2262|
2263|# Now you can use the shortcuts on the CLI:
2264|# --option2 sets 'option', --list_option2 sets 'list_option'
2265|```
2266|
2267|**Nested Example:**
2268|
2269|```py
2270|from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
2271|
2272|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
2273|
2274|
2275|class TwiceNested(BaseModel):
2276|    option: str = Field(default='foo')
2277|
2278|
2279|class Nested(BaseModel):
2280|    twice_nested_option: TwiceNested = TwiceNested()
2281|    option: str = Field(default='foo')
2282|
2283|
2284|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2285|    nested: Nested = Nested()
2286|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
2287|        cli_shortcuts={
2288|            'nested.option': 'option2',
2289|            'nested.twice_nested_option.option': 'twice_nested_option',
2290|        }
2291|    )
2292|
2293|
2294|# Now you can use --option2 to set nested.option and --twice_nested_option to set nested.twice_nested_option.option
2295|```
2296|
2297|If a shortcut collides (is mapped to multiple fields), it will apply to the first matching field in the model.
2298|
2299|### Integrating with Existing Parsers
2300|
2301|A CLI settings source can be integrated with existing parsers by overriding the default CLI settings source with a user
2302|defined one that specifies the `root_parser` object.
2303|
2304|```py
2305|import sys
2306|from argparse import ArgumentParser
2307|
2308|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, CliApp, CliSettingsSource
2309|
2310|parser = ArgumentParser()
2311|parser.add_argument('--food', choices=['pear', 'kiwi', 'lime'])
2312|
2313|
2314|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2315|    name: str = 'Bob'
2316|
2317|
2318|# Set existing `parser` as the `root_parser` object for the user defined settings source
2319|cli_settings = CliSettingsSource(Settings, root_parser=parser)
2320|
2321|# Parse and load CLI settings from the command line into the settings source.
2322|sys.argv = ['example.py', '--food', 'kiwi', '--name', 'waldo']
2323|s = CliApp.run(Settings, cli_settings_source=cli_settings)
2324|print(s.model_dump())
2325|#> {'name': 'waldo'}
2326|
2327|# Load CLI settings from pre-parsed arguments. i.e., the parsing occurs elsewhere and we
2328|# just need to load the pre-parsed args into the settings source.
2329|parsed_args = parser.parse_args(['--food', 'kiwi', '--name', 'ralph'])
2330|s = CliApp.run(Settings, cli_args=parsed_args, cli_settings_source=cli_settings)
2331|print(s.model_dump())
2332|#> {'name': 'ralph'}
2333|```
2334|
2335|A `CliSettingsSource` connects with a `root_parser` object by using parser methods to add `settings_cls` fields as
2336|command line arguments. The `CliSettingsSource` internal parser representation is based on the `argparse` library, and
2337|therefore, requires parser methods that support the same attributes as their `argparse` counterparts. The available
2338|parser methods that can be customised, along with their argparse counterparts (the defaults), are listed below:
2339|
2340|* `parse_args_method` - (`argparse.ArgumentParser.parse_args`)
2341|* `add_argument_method` - (`argparse.ArgumentParser.add_argument`)
2342|* `add_argument_group_method` - (`argparse.ArgumentParser.add_argument_group`)
2343|* `add_parser_method` - (`argparse._SubParsersAction.add_parser`)
2344|* `add_subparsers_method` - (`argparse.ArgumentParser.add_subparsers`)
2345|* `format_help_method` - (`argparse.ArgumentParser.format_help`)
2346|* `formatter_class` - (`argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter`)
2347|
2348|For a non-argparse parser the parser methods can be set to `None` if not supported. The CLI settings will only raise an
2349|error when connecting to the root parser if a parser method is necessary but set to `None`.
2350|
2351|!!! note
2352|    The `formatter_class` is only applied to subcommands. The `CliSettingsSource` never touches or modifies any of the
2353|    external parser settings to avoid breaking changes. Since subcommands reside on their own internal parser trees, we
2354|    can safely apply the `formatter_class` settings without breaking the external parser logic.
2355|
2356|## Secrets
2357|
2358|Placing secret values in files is a common pattern to provide sensitive configuration to an application.
2359|
2360|A secret file follows the same principal as a dotenv file except it only contains a single value and the file name
2361|is used as the key. A secret file will look like the following:
2362|
2363|``` title="/var/run/database_password"
2364|super_secret_database_password
2365|```
2366|
2367|Once you have your secret files, *pydantic* supports loading it in two ways:
2368|
2369|1. Setting the `secrets_dir` on `model_config` in a `BaseSettings` class to the directory where your secret files are stored.
2370|   ````py hl_lines="4 5 6 7"
2371|   from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
2372|
2373|
2374|   class Settings(BaseSettings):
2375|       model_config = SettingsConfigDict(secrets_dir='/var/run')
2376|
2377|       database_password: str
2378|   ````
2379|2. Instantiating the `BaseSettings` derived class with the `_secrets_dir` keyword argument:
2380|   ````
2381|   settings = Settings(_secrets_dir='/var/run')
2382|   ````
2383|
2384|In either case, the value of the passed argument can be any valid directory, either absolute or relative to the
2385|current working directory. **Note that a non existent directory will only generate a warning**.
2386|From there, *pydantic* will handle everything for you by loading in your variables and validating them.
2387|
2388|Even when using a secrets directory, *pydantic* will still read environment variables from a dotenv file or the environment,
2389|**a dotenv file and environment variables will always take priority over values loaded from the secrets directory**.
2390|
2391|Passing a file path via the `_secrets_dir` keyword argument on instantiation (method 2) will override
2392|the value (if any) set on the `model_config` class.
2393|
2394|If you need to load settings from multiple secrets directories, you can pass multiple paths as a tuple or list. Just like for `env_file`, values from subsequent paths override previous ones.
2395|
2396|````python
2397|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
2398|
2399|
2400|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2401|    # files in '/run/secrets' take priority over '/var/run'
2402|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(secrets_dir=('/var/run', '/run/secrets'))
2403|
2404|    database_password: str
2405|````
2406|
2407|If any of `secrets_dir` is missing, it is ignored, and warning is shown. If any of `secrets_dir` is a file, error is raised.
2408|
2409|
2410|### Use Case: Docker Secrets
2411|
2412|Docker Secrets can be used to provide sensitive configuration to an application running in a Docker container.
2413|To use these secrets in a *pydantic* application the process is simple. More information regarding creating, managing
2414|and using secrets in Docker see the official
2415|[Docker documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/secret/).
2416|
2417|First, define your `Settings` class with a `SettingsConfigDict` that specifies the secrets directory.
2418|
2419|```py hl_lines="4 5 6 7"
2420|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
2421|
2422|
2423|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2424|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(secrets_dir='/run/secrets')
2425|
2426|    my_secret_data: str
2427|```
2428|
2429|!!! note
2430|    By default [Docker uses `/run/secrets`](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/secrets/#how-docker-manages-secrets)
2431|    as the target mount point. If you want to use a different location, change `Config.secrets_dir` accordingly.
2432|
2433|Then, create your secret via the Docker CLI
2434|```bash
2435|printf "This is a secret" | docker secret create my_secret_data -
2436|```
2437|
2438|Last, run your application inside a Docker container and supply your newly created secret
2439|```bash
2440|docker service create --name pydantic-with-secrets --secret my_secret_data pydantic-app:latest
2441|```
2442|
2443|## Nested Secrets
2444|
2445|The default secrets implementation, `SecretsSettingsSource`, has behaviour that is not always desired or sufficient.
2446|For example, the default implementation does not support secret fields in nested submodels.
2447|
2448|`NestedSecretsSettingsSource` can be used as a drop-in replacement to `SecretsSettingsSource` to adjust the default behaviour.
2449|It is opt-in: you have to configure it explicitly via the `settings_customise_sources` hook (see the examples below),
2450|otherwise `BaseSettings` keeps using the default `SecretsSettingsSource`.
2451|All differences are summarized in the table below.
2452|
2453|| `SecretsSettingsSource`                                                                                                                                         | `NestedSecretsSettingsSource`                                                                                                    |
2454||-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
2455|| Secret fields must belong to a top level model.                                                                                                                 | Secrets can be fields of nested models.                                                                                           |
2456|| Secret files can be placed in `secrets_dir`s only.                                                                                                              | Secret files can be placed in subdirectories for nested models.                                                                   |
2457|| Secret files discovery is based on the same configuration options that are used by `EnvSettingsSource`: `case_sensitive`, `env_nested_delimiter`, `env_prefix`. | Default options are respected, but can be overridden with `secrets_case_sensitive`, `secrets_nested_delimiter`, `secrets_prefix`. |
2458|| When `secrets_dir` is missing on the file system, a warning is generated.                                                                                       | Use `secrets_dir_missing` options to choose whether to issue warning, raise error, or silently ignore.                            |
2459|
2460|### Use Case: Plain Directory Layout
2461|
2462|```text
2463|📂 secrets
2464|├── 📄 app_key
2465|└── 📄 db_passwd
2466|```
2467|
2468|In the example below, secrets nested delimiter `'_'` is different from env nested delimiter `'__'`.
2469|Value for `Settings.db.user` can be passed in env variable `MY_DB__USER`.
2470|
2471|```py
2472|from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
2473|
2474|from pydantic_settings import (
2475|    BaseSettings,
2476|    NestedSecretsSettingsSource,
2477|    SettingsConfigDict,
2478|)
2479|

2481|class AppSettings(BaseModel):
2482|    key: SecretStr
2483|
2484|
2485|class DbSettings(BaseModel):
2486|    user: str
2487|    passwd: SecretStr
2488|
2489|
2490|class Settings(BaseSettings):
2491|    app: AppSettings
2492|    db: DbSettings
2493|
2494|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
2495|        env_prefix='MY_',
2496|        env_nested_delimiter='__',
2497|        secrets_dir='secrets',
2498|        secrets_nested_delimiter='_',
2499|    )
2500|
2501|    @classmethod
2502|    def settings_customise_sources(
2503|        cls,
2504|        settings_cls,
2505|        init_settings,
2506|        env_settings,
2507|        dotenv_settings,
2508|        file_secret_settings,
2509|    ):
2510|        return (
2511|            init_settings,
2512|            env_settings,
2513|            dotenv_settings,
2514|            NestedSecretsSettingsSource(file_secret_settings),
2515|        )
2516|```

2636|### Configuration Options
2637|
2638|!!! note
2639|    Apart from `secrets_dir`, which is shared with `SecretsSettingsSource`, all of the options below are read
2640|    only by `NestedSecretsSettingsSource`. They have no effect unless you add that source to your settings
2641|    sources via the `settings_customise_sources` hook, as shown in the examples above — the default
2642|    `SecretsSettingsSource` ignores them. Setting one of them without configuring the source raises a
2643|    `UserWarning` telling you it will be ignored.
2644|
2645|#### secrets_dir
2646|
2647|Path to secrets directory, same as `SecretsSettingsSource.secrets_dir`. If `list`, the last match wins.
2648|If `secrets_dir` is passed in both source constructor and model config, values are not merged (constructor wins).
2649|When wrapping a `SecretsSettingsSource`, an explicit `secrets_dir` also takes precedence over the wrapped source's
2650|directory, including `Settings(_secrets_dir=...)`; omit it to inherit them.
2651|Pass an empty list to disable loading from secrets directories.
2652|
2653|#### secrets_dir_missing
2654|
2655|If `secrets_dir` does not exist, original `SecretsSettingsSource` issues a warning.
2656|However, this may be undesirable, for example if we don't mount Docker Secrets in e.g. dev environment.
2657|Use `secrets_dir_missing` to choose:
2658|
2659|* `'ok'` — do nothing if `secrets_dir` does not exist
2660|* `'warn'` (default) — print warning, same as `SecretsSettingsSource`
2661|* `'error'` — raise `SettingsError`
2662|
2663|If multiple `secrets_dir` passed, the same `secrets_dir_missing` action applies to each of them.
2664|
2665|#### secrets_dir_max_size
2666|
2667|Limit the size of `secrets_dir` for security reasons, defaults to `SECRETS_DIR_MAX_SIZE` equal to 16 MiB.
2668|
2669|`NestedSecretsSettingsSource` is a thin wrapper around `EnvSettingsSource`,
2670|which loads all potential secrets on initialization. This could lead to `MemoryError` if we mount
2671|a large file under `secrets_dir`.
2672|
2673|If multiple `secrets_dir` passed, the limit applies to each directory independently.
2674|
2675|#### secrets_case_sensitive
2676|
2677|Same as `case_sensitive`, but works for secrets only. If not specified, defaults to `case_sensitive`.
2678|
2679|Unlike `case_sensitive` for environment variables, this option is honored on every platform.
2680|`os.environ` is case-insensitive on Windows, so `EnvSettingsSource` falls back to
2681|case-insensitive matching there; secrets are files and keep their case, so no such fallback
2682|applies.
2683|
2684|#### secrets_nested_delimiter
2685|
2686|Same as `env_nested_delimiter`, but works for secrets only. If not specified, defaults to `env_nested_delimiter`.
2687|This option is used to implement _nested secrets directory_ layout and allows you to do even nasty things
2688|like `/run/secrets/model/delim/nested1/delim/nested2`.
2689|
2690|#### secrets_nested_subdir
2691|
2692|Boolean flag to turn on _nested secrets directory_ mode, `False` by default. If `True`, sets `secrets_nested_delimiter`
2693|to `os.sep`. Raises `SettingsError` if `secrets_nested_delimiter` is already specified.
2694|
2695|#### secrets_prefix
2696|
2697|Secret path prefix, similar to `env_prefix`, but works for secrets only. Defaults to `env_prefix`
2698|if not specified. Works in both plain and nested directory modes, like
2699|`'/run/secrets/prefix_model__nested'` and `'/run/secrets/prefix_model/nested'`.
2700|
2701|
2702|## AWS Secrets Manager
2703|
2704|You must set one parameter:
2705|
2706|- `secret_id`: The AWS secret id
2707|
2708|You must have the same naming convention in the key value in secret as in the field name. For example, if the key in secret is named `SqlServerPassword`, the field name must be the same. You can use an alias too.
2709|
2710|In AWS Secrets Manager, nested models are supported with the `--` separator in the key name. For example, `SqlServer--Password`.
2711|
2712|Arrays (e.g. `MySecret--0`, `MySecret--1`) are not supported.
2713|
2714|```py
2715|import os
2716|
2717|from pydantic import BaseModel
2718|
2719|from pydantic_settings import (
2720|    AWSSecretsManagerSettingsSource,
2721|    BaseSettings,
2722|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2723|)
2724|
2725|
2726|class SubModel(BaseModel):
2727|    a: str
2728|
2729|
2730|class AWSSecretsManagerSettings(BaseSettings):
2731|    foo: str
2732|    bar: int
2733|    sub: SubModel
2734|
2735|    @classmethod
2736|    def settings_customise_sources(
2737|        cls,
2738|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
2739|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2740|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2741|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2742|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2743|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
2744|        aws_secrets_manager_settings = AWSSecretsManagerSettingsSource(
2745|            settings_cls,
2746|            os.environ['AWS_SECRETS_MANAGER_SECRET_ID'],
2747|        )
2748|        return (
2749|            init_settings,
2750|            env_settings,
2751|            dotenv_settings,
2752|            file_secret_settings,
2753|            aws_secrets_manager_settings,
2754|        )
2755|```

2757|## AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
2758|
2759|You may set the following parameters:
2760|
2761|- `ssm_path`: The path hierarchy the parameters live under, for example `/prod/my-app`. Must start with `/`, and defaults to `/`.
2762|
2763|All parameters below `ssm_path` are read recursively with the [`get_parameters_by_path`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/ssm/client/get_parameters_by_path.html)
2764|API (with `WithDecryption=True`, so `SecureString` parameters are decrypted). The `ssm_path` prefix is stripped from
2765|each parameter name, and the remaining path is used as the field name.
2766|
2767|Because Parameter Store already uses a `/`-delimited hierarchy, nested models are supported with the `/` separator.
2768|For example, a parameter named `/prod/my-app/sub/a` populates the `a` field of the `sub` model. You must have the same
2769|naming convention in the field name as in the parameter name, or use an alias.
2770|
2771|```py
2772|import os
2773|
2774|from pydantic import BaseModel
2775|
2776|from pydantic_settings import (
2777|    AWSSystemsManagerSettingsSource,
2778|    BaseSettings,
2779|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2780|)
2781|
2782|
2783|class SubModel(BaseModel):
2784|    a: str
2785|
2786|

2788|    foo: str
2789|    bar: int
2790|    sub: SubModel
2791|
2792|    @classmethod
2793|    def settings_customise_sources(
2794|        cls,
2795|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
2796|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2797|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2798|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2799|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2800|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
2801|        aws_systems_manager_settings = AWSSystemsManagerSettingsSource(
2802|            settings_cls,
2803|            os.environ['AWS_SSM_PATH'],
2804|        )
2805|        return (
2806|            init_settings,
2807|            env_settings,
2808|            dotenv_settings,
2809|            file_secret_settings,
2810|            aws_systems_manager_settings,
2811|        )
2812|```

2814|## Azure Key Vault
2815|
2816|You must set two parameters:
2817|
2818|- `url`: For example, `https://my-resource.vault.azure.net/`.
2819|- `credential`: If you use `DefaultAzureCredential`, in local you can execute `az login` to get your identity credentials. The identity must have a role assignment (the recommended one is `Key Vault Secrets User`), so you can access the secrets.
2820|
2821|You must have the same naming convention in the field name as in the Key Vault secret name. For example, if the secret is named `SqlServerPassword`, the field name must be the same. You can use an alias too.
2822|
2823|In Key Vault, nested models are supported with the `--` separator. For example, `SqlServer--Password`.
2824|
2825|Key Vault arrays (e.g. `MySecret--0`, `MySecret--1`) are not supported.
2826|
2827|```py
2828|import os
2829|
2830|from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
2831|from pydantic import BaseModel
2832|
2833|from pydantic_settings import (
2834|    AzureKeyVaultSettingsSource,
2835|    BaseSettings,
2836|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2837|)
2838|
2839|
2840|class SubModel(BaseModel):
2841|    a: str
2842|
2843|
2844|class AzureKeyVaultSettings(BaseSettings):
2845|    foo: str
2846|    bar: int
2847|    sub: SubModel
2848|
2849|    @classmethod
2850|    def settings_customise_sources(
2851|        cls,
2852|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
2853|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2854|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2855|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2856|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2857|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
2858|        az_key_vault_settings = AzureKeyVaultSettingsSource(
2859|            settings_cls,
2860|            os.environ['AZURE_KEY_VAULT_URL'],
2861|            DefaultAzureCredential(),
2862|        )
2863|        return (
2864|            init_settings,
2865|            env_settings,
2866|            dotenv_settings,
2867|            file_secret_settings,
2868|            az_key_vault_settings,
2869|        )
2870|```
2871|
2872|### Snake case conversion
2873|
2874|The Azure Key Vault source accepts a `snake_case_conversion` option, disabled by default, to convert Key Vault secret names by mapping them to Python's snake_case field names, without the need to use aliases.
2875|
2876|```py
2877|import os
2878|
2879|from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
2880|
2881|from pydantic_settings import (
2882|    AzureKeyVaultSettingsSource,
2883|    BaseSettings,
2884|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2885|)
2886|
2887|
2888|class AzureKeyVaultSettings(BaseSettings):
2889|    my_setting: str
2890|
2891|    @classmethod
2892|    def settings_customise_sources(
2893|        cls,
2894|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
2895|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2896|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2897|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2898|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2899|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
2900|        az_key_vault_settings = AzureKeyVaultSettingsSource(
2901|            settings_cls,
2902|            os.environ['AZURE_KEY_VAULT_URL'],
2903|            DefaultAzureCredential(),
2904|            snake_case_conversion=True,
2905|        )
2906|        return (az_key_vault_settings,)
2907|```
2908|
2909|This setup will load Azure Key Vault secrets (e.g., `MySetting`, `mySetting`, `my-secret` or `MY-SECRET`), mapping them to the snake case version (`my_setting` in this case).
2910|
2911|### Dash to underscore mapping
2912|
2913|The Azure Key Vault source accepts a `dash_to_underscore` option, disabled by default, to support Key Vault kebab-case secret names by mapping them to Python's snake_case field names. When enabled, dashes (`-`) in secret names are mapped to underscores (`_`) in field names during validation.
2914|
2915|This mapping applies only to *field names*, not to aliases. Use `--` to separate nested model fields; dashes in their names are mapped the same way, while dictionary keys are kept as-is.
2916|
2917|```py
2918|import os
2919|
2920|from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
2921|from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
2922|
2923|from pydantic_settings import (
2924|    AzureKeyVaultSettingsSource,
2925|    BaseSettings,
2926|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2927|)
2928|
2929|
2930|class DatabaseSettings(BaseModel):
2931|    sql_password: str
2932|
2933|
2934|class AzureKeyVaultSettings(BaseSettings):
2935|    field_with_underscore: str
2936|    field_with_alias: str = Field(..., alias='Alias-With-Dashes')
2937|    database: DatabaseSettings
2938|
2939|    @classmethod
2940|    def settings_customise_sources(
2941|        cls,
2942|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
2943|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2944|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2945|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2946|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2947|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
2948|        az_key_vault_settings = AzureKeyVaultSettingsSource(
2949|            settings_cls,
2950|            os.environ['AZURE_KEY_VAULT_URL'],
2951|            DefaultAzureCredential(),
2952|            dash_to_underscore=True,
2953|        )
2954|        return (az_key_vault_settings,)
2955|```
2956|
2957|This setup will load Azure Key Vault secrets named `field-with-underscore`, `Alias-With-Dashes` and `database--sql-password`, mapping them to the `field_with_underscore`, `field_with_alias` and `database.sql_password` fields, respectively.
2958|
2959|!!! tip
2960|    Alternatively, you can configure an [alias_generator](alias.md#using-alias-generators) to map PascalCase secrets.
2961|
2962|## Google Cloud Secret Manager
2963|
2964|Google Cloud Secret Manager allows you to store, manage, and access sensitive information as secrets in Google Cloud Platform. This integration lets you retrieve secrets directly from GCP Secret Manager for use in your Pydantic settings.
2965|
2966|### Installation
2967|
2968|The Google Cloud Secret Manager integration requires additional dependencies:
2969|
2970|```bash
2971|pip install "pydantic-settings[gcp-secret-manager]"
2972|```
2973|
2974|### Basic Usage
2975|
2976|To use Google Cloud Secret Manager, you need to:
2977|
2978|1. Create a `GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource`. (See [GCP Authentication](#gcp-authentication) for authentication options.)
2979|2. Add this source to your settings customization pipeline
2980|
2981|   ```py
2982|   from pydantic import BaseModel
2983|
2984|   from pydantic_settings import (
2985|       BaseSettings,
2986|       GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource,
2987|       PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
2988|       SettingsConfigDict,
2989|   )
2990|
2991|
2992|   class Database(BaseModel):
2993|       password: str
2994|       user: str
2995|
2996|
2997|   class Settings(BaseSettings):
2998|       database: Database
2999|
3000|       model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter='__')
3001|
3002|       @classmethod
3003|       def settings_customise_sources(
3004|           cls,
3005|           settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3006|           init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3007|           env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3008|           dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3009|           file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3010|       ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3011|           # Create the GCP Secret Manager settings source
3012|           gcp_settings = GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource(
3013|               settings_cls,
3014|               # If not provided, will use google.auth.default()
3015|               # to get credentials from the environment
3016|               # credentials=your_credentials,
3017|               # If not provided, will use google.auth.default()
3018|               # to get project_id from the environment
3019|               project_id='your-gcp-project-id',
3020|           )
3021|
3022|           return (
3023|               init_settings,
3024|               env_settings,
3025|               dotenv_settings,
3026|               file_secret_settings,
3027|               gcp_settings,
3028|           )
3029|   ```
3030|
3031|### GCP Authentication
3032|
3033|The `GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource` supports several authentication methods:
3034|
3035|1. **Default credentials** - If you don't provide credentials or project ID, it will use [`google.auth.default()`](https://google-auth.readthedocs.io/en/master/reference/google.auth.html#google.auth.default) to obtain them. This works with:
3036|
3037|   - Service account credentials from `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` environment variable
3038|   - User credentials from `gcloud auth application-default login`
3039|   - Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, or Cloud Functions default service accounts
3040|
3041|2. **Explicit credentials** - You can also provide `credentials` directly. e.g. `sa_credentials = google.oauth2.service_account.Credentials.from_service_account_file('path/to/service-account.json')` and then `GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource(credentials=sa_credentials)`
3042|
3043|### Project ID resolution
3044|
3045|The `project_id` is resolved lazily when the source is read, in the following order of precedence:
3046|
3047|1. the explicit `project_id` argument if it was passed
3048|2. the value resolved by a previous (higher priority) settings source - by default the `project_id` field, configurable via the `project_id_field` argument
3049|3. [`google.auth.default()`](https://google-auth.readthedocs.io/en/master/reference/google.auth.html#google.auth.default)
3050|
3051|This lets the project be supplied by another settings source (for example an environment variable or an init argument) instead of being hardcoded. For example, with `GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource(settings_cls, project_id_field='gcp_project')` the source uses the `gcp_project` value resolved by an earlier source as its project.
3052|
3053|`project_id_field` must match the key that the earlier source uses in `current_state` — this is typically the field's preferred alias. For example, if your settings model has `gcp_project: str = Field(alias='GCP_PROJECT')`, use `project_id_field='GCP_PROJECT'` (the alias), not `'gcp_project'` (the Python attribute name).
3054|
3055|### Nested Models
3056|
3057|For nested models, Secret Manager supports the `env_nested_delimiter` setting as long as it complies with the [naming rules](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/creating-and-accessing-secrets#create-a-secret). In the example above, you would create secrets named `database__password` and `database__user` in Secret Manager.
3058|
3059|### Secret Versions
3060|
3061|By default, `GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource` uses the "latest" version of secrets.
3062|You can specify a different version using the `SecretVersion` annotation.
3063|
3064|```py
3065|from typing import Annotated
3066|
3067|from pydantic import Field
3068|
3069|from pydantic_settings import (
3070|    BaseSettings,
3071|    GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource,
3072|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3073|)
3074|from pydantic_settings.sources.types import SecretVersion
3075|
3076|
3077|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3078|    # This will use the "latest" version
3079|    my_secret: str = Field(alias='my-secret')
3080|    # This will use version "1"
3081|    my_secret_v1: Annotated[str, Field(alias='my-secret'), SecretVersion('1')]
3082|
3083|    @classmethod
3084|    def settings_customise_sources(
3085|        cls,
3086|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3087|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3088|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3089|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3090|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3091|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3092|        return (
3093|            GoogleSecretManagerSettingsSource(settings_cls, project_id='my-project'),
3094|            init_settings,
3095|            env_settings,
3096|            dotenv_settings,
3097|            file_secret_settings,
3098|        )
3099|```
3100|
3101|!!! note
3102|    If you have multiple fields pointing to the same secret (alias) but with different versions, you MUST enable `populate_by_name=True` (or `validate_by_name=True`) in `SettingsConfigDict`.
3103|
3104|
3105|### Important Notes
3106|
3107|1. **Case Sensitivity**: By default, secret names are case-sensitive.
3108|    *   If you set `case_sensitive=False`, `pydantic-settings` will attempt to resolve secrets in a case-insensitive manner. It prioritizes exact matches over case-insensitive matches. For some examples of this, imagine `case_sensitive=False` and the model attribute is named `my_secret`:
3109|        * If Google Secret Manager has both `MY_SECRET` and `my_secret` defined - the value of `my_secret` will be returned.
3110|        * If Google Secret Manager has `MY_SECRET`, `My_Secret`, and `my_Secret` defined - a warning will be raised and the value of `my_Secret` will be returned - as the secret names are first sorted in ASCII sort order (where lowercased letters are greater than upper case letters) and the last one is chosen (which would be `my_Secret` in this case).
3111|2. **Secret Naming**: Create secrets in Google Secret Manager with names that match your field names (including any prefix). According to the [Secret Manager documentation](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/creating-and-accessing-secrets#create-a-secret), a secret name can contain uppercase and lowercase letters, numerals, hyphens, and underscores. The maximum allowed length for a name is 255 characters.
3112|
3113|For more details on creating and managing secrets in Google Cloud Secret Manager, see the [official Google Cloud documentation](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs).
3114|
3115|## Other settings source
3116|
3117|Other settings sources are available for common configuration files:
3118|
3119|- `JsonConfigSettingsSource` using `json_file` and `json_file_encoding` arguments
3120|- `PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource` using *(optional)* `pyproject_toml_depth` and *(optional)* `pyproject_toml_table_header` arguments
3121|- `TomlConfigSettingsSource` using `toml_file` argument and *(optional)* `toml_table_header` argument
3122|- `YamlConfigSettingsSource` using `yaml_file` and yaml_file_encoding arguments
3123|
3124|To use them, you can use the same mechanism described [here](#customise-settings-sources).
3125|
3126|```py
3127|from pydantic import BaseModel
3128|
3129|from pydantic_settings import (
3130|    BaseSettings,
3131|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3132|    SettingsConfigDict,
3133|    TomlConfigSettingsSource,
3134|)
3135|
3136|
3137|class Nested(BaseModel):
3138|    nested_field: str
3139|
3140|
3141|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3142|    foobar: str
3143|    nested: Nested
3144|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(toml_file='config.toml')
3145|
3146|    @classmethod
3147|    def settings_customise_sources(
3148|        cls,
3149|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3150|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3151|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3152|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3153|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3154|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3155|        return (TomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls),)
3156|```
3157|
3158|This will be able to read the following "config.toml" file, located in your working directory:
3159|
3160|```toml
3161|foobar = "Hello"
3162|[nested]
3163|nested_field = "world!"
3164|```
3165|
3166|You can also provide multiple files by providing a list of paths.
3167|
3168|```py
3169|from pydantic import BaseModel
3170|
3171|from pydantic_settings import (
3172|    BaseSettings,
3173|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3174|    SettingsConfigDict,
3175|    TomlConfigSettingsSource,
3176|)
3177|
3178|
3179|class Nested(BaseModel):
3180|    foo: int
3181|    bar: int = 0
3182|
3183|
3184|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3185|    hello: str
3186|    nested: Nested
3187|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
3188|        toml_file=['config.default.toml', 'config.custom.toml']
3189|    )
3190|
3191|    @classmethod
3192|    def settings_customise_sources(
3193|        cls,
3194|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3195|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3196|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3197|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3198|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3199|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3200|        return (TomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls),)
3201|```
3202|
3203|The following two configuration files
3204|
3205|```toml
3206|# config.default.toml
3207|hello = "World"
3208|
3209|[nested]
3210|foo = 1
3211|bar = 2
3212|```
3213|
3214|```toml
3215|# config.custom.toml
3216|[nested]
3217|foo = 3
3218|```
3219|
3220|are equivalent to
3221|
3222|```toml
3223|hello = "world"
3224|
3225|[nested]
3226|foo = 3
3227|```
3228|
3229|The files are merged shallowly in increasing order of priority. To enable deep merging, set `deep_merge=True` on the source directly.
3230|
3231|!!! warning
3232|    The `deep_merge` option is **not available** through the `SettingsConfigDict`.
3233|
3234|!!! note
3235|    In addition to `str` and `pathlib.Path`, the `json_file`, `toml_file`, and `yaml_file` options also accept a
3236|    [`Traversable`][importlib.resources.abc.Traversable], such as the result of `importlib.resources.files(...).joinpath(...)`.
3237|    This makes it possible to load a configuration file that is packaged inside your distribution, including cases where the
3238|    resource does not live on the filesystem (e.g. inside a zip/wheel).
3239|
3240|```py
3241|from pydantic import BaseModel
3242|
3243|from pydantic_settings import (
3244|    BaseSettings,
3245|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3246|    SettingsConfigDict,
3247|    TomlConfigSettingsSource,
3248|)
3249|
3250|
3251|class Nested(BaseModel):
3252|    foo: int
3253|    bar: int = 0
3254|
3255|
3256|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3257|    hello: str
3258|    nested: Nested
3259|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
3260|        toml_file=['config.default.toml', 'config.custom.toml']
3261|    )
3262|
3263|    @classmethod
3264|    def settings_customise_sources(
3265|        cls,
3266|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3267|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3268|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3269|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3270|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3271|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3272|        return (TomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls, deep_merge=True),)
3273|```
3274|
3275|With deep merge enabled, the following two configuration files
3276|
3277|```toml
3278|# config.default.toml
3279|hello = "World"
3280|
3281|[nested]
3282|foo = 1
3283|bar = 2
3284|```
3285|
3286|```toml
3287|# config.custom.toml
3288|[nested]
3289|foo = 3
3290|```
3291|
3292|are equivalent to
3293|
3294|```toml
3295|hello = "world"
3296|
3297|[nested]
3298|foo = 3
3299|bar = 2
3300|```
3301|
3302|If you want to load from a specific table in the file, you can provide `toml_table_header` as a tuple of header parts. For example, `toml_table_header=('my-table',)` will load variables from the `[my-table]` table.
3303|
3304|Passing `toml_table_header` directly to `TomlConfigSettingsSource` overrides the model configuration. Use `toml_table_header=()` to load from the root of the file, even when the model configures a table header. Omitting the argument or passing `None` uses the model configuration.
3305|
3306|```python
3307|from pydantic_settings import (
3308|    BaseSettings,
3309|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3310|    SettingsConfigDict,
3311|    TomlConfigSettingsSource,
3312|)
3313|
3314|
3315|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3316|    field: str
3317|
3318|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
3319|        toml_file='config.toml', toml_table_header=('my-table',)
3320|    )
3321|
3322|    @classmethod
3323|    def settings_customise_sources(
3324|        cls,
3325|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3326|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3327|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3328|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3329|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3330|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3331|        return (TomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls),)
3332|```
3333|
3334|This will allow you to read the following TOML file:
3335|```toml
3336|# config.toml
3337|[my-table]
3338|field = "value from my-table"
3339|```

3341|### pyproject.toml
3342|
3343|"pyproject.toml" is a standardized file for providing configuration values in Python projects.
3344|[PEP 518](https://peps.python.org/pep-0518/#tool-table) defines a `[tool]` table that can be used to provide arbitrary tool configuration.
3345|While encouraged to use the `[tool]` table, `PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource` can be used to load variables from any location with in "pyproject.toml" file.
3346|
3347|This is controlled by providing `SettingsConfigDict(pyproject_toml_table_header=tuple[str, ...])` where the value is a tuple of header parts.
3348|By default, `pyproject_toml_table_header=('tool', 'pydantic-settings')` which will load variables from the `[tool.pydantic-settings]` table.
3349|
3350|```python
3351|from pydantic_settings import (
3352|    BaseSettings,
3353|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3354|    PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource,
3355|    SettingsConfigDict,
3356|)
3357|
3358|
3359|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3360|    """Example loading values from the table used by default."""
3361|
3362|    field: str
3363|
3364|    @classmethod
3365|    def settings_customise_sources(
3366|        cls,
3367|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3368|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3369|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3370|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3371|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3372|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3373|        return (PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls),)
3374|
3375|
3376|class SomeTableSettings(Settings):
3377|    """Example loading values from a user defined table."""
3378|
3379|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
3380|        pyproject_toml_table_header=('tool', 'some-table')
3381|    )
3382|
3383|
3384|class RootSettings(Settings):
3385|    """Example loading values from the root of a pyproject.toml file."""
3386|
3387|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(extra='ignore', pyproject_toml_table_header=())
3388|```
3389|
3390|This will be able to read the following "pyproject.toml" file, located in your working directory, resulting in `Settings(field='default-table')`, `SomeTableSettings(field='some-table')`, & `RootSettings(field='root')`:
3391|
3392|```toml
3393|field = "root"
3394|
3395|[tool.pydantic-settings]
3396|field = "default-table"
3397|
3398|[tool.some-table]
3399|field = "some-table"
3400|```
3401|
3402|By default, `PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource` will only look for a "pyproject.toml" in the your current working directory.
3403|However, there are two options to change this behavior.
3404|
3405|* `SettingsConfigDict(pyproject_toml_depth=<int>)` can be provided to check `<int>` number of directories **up** in the directory tree for a "pyproject.toml" if one is not found in the current working directory.
3406|  By default, no parent directories are checked.
3407|* An explicit file path can be provided to the source when it is instantiated (e.g. `PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls, Path('~/.config').resolve() / 'pyproject.toml')`).
3408|  If a file path is provided this way, it will be treated as absolute (no other locations are checked).

3413|from pydantic_settings import (
3414|    BaseSettings,
3415|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3416|    PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource,
3417|    SettingsConfigDict,
3418|)
3419|

3422|    """Example of discovering a pyproject.toml in parent directories in not in `Path.cwd()`."""
3423|

3425|
3426|    @classmethod
3427|    def settings_customise_sources(
3428|        cls,
3429|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3430|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3431|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3432|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3433|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3434|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3435|        return (PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource(settings_cls),)
3436|
3437|
3438|class ExplicitFilePathSettings(BaseSettings):
3439|    """Example of explicitly providing the path to the file to load."""
3440|
3441|    field: str
3442|

3445|        cls,
3446|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3447|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3448|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3449|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,

3459|## Field value priority
3460|
3461|In the case where a value is specified for the same `Settings` field in multiple ways,
3462|the selected value is determined as follows (in descending order of priority):
3463|
3464|1. If `cli_parse_args` is enabled, arguments passed in at the CLI.
3465|2. Arguments passed to the `Settings` class initialiser.
3466|3. Environment variables, e.g. `my_prefix_special_function` as described above.
3467|4. Variables loaded from a dotenv (`.env`) file.
3468|5. Variables loaded from the secrets directory.
3469|6. The default field values for the `Settings` model.
3470|
3471|## Debugging settings sources
3472|
3473|When several sources are enabled, it can be hard to tell which source a given value came from — and
3474|why. Setting the `PYDANTIC_SETTINGS_DEBUG` environment variable to a truthy value (`1`, `true`, `yes`,
3475|or `on`) makes pydantic-settings log, at `DEBUG` level, the dictionary collected by every source in
3476|priority order (highest first):
3477|
3478|```bash
3479|PYDANTIC_SETTINGS_DEBUG=1 python your_app.py
3480|```
3481|
3482|The output is emitted on the `pydantic_settings` logger, so make sure `DEBUG`-level logging is enabled
3483|(for example via `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)`). A typical report looks like:
3484|
3485|```
3486|Resolving settings for 'Settings' (sources in priority order, highest first):
3487|  InitSettingsSource: {'port': 9000}
3488|  EnvSettingsSource: {'name': 'from_env'}
3489|  DotEnvSettingsSource: {}
3490|  SecretsSettingsSource: {}
3491|  DefaultSettingsSource: {}
3492|```
3493|
3494|Sources are listed from highest to lowest priority and merged using a deep update: higher-priority sources override lower-priority ones.
3495|For nested structures, lower-priority sources may still contribute missing sub-keys even when the top-level key is present in a higher-priority source.
3496|
3497|The same flag also traces file resolution, so you can see which dotenv and secret files were actually
3498|found and loaded — helpful when running the same code from a different working directory silently
3499|yields defaults because a relative `.env` path didn't resolve:
3500|
3501|```
3502|Env file not found, skipping: /home/app/.env.production
3503|Loading env file: /home/app/.env
3504|Secret file not found, skipping: /run/secrets/api_key
3505|```
3506|
3507|!!! warning
3508|    The debug output includes the values loaded from every source, which may contain secrets loaded
3509|    from environment variables, dotenv files, or the secrets directory. Only enable it in a trusted
3510|    debugging context, and avoid leaving it on in production.
3511|
3512|## Customise settings sources
3513|
3514|If the default order of priority doesn't match your needs, it's possible to change it by overriding
3515|the `settings_customise_sources` method of your `Settings` .
3516|
3517|`settings_customise_sources` takes four callables as arguments and returns any number of callables as a tuple.
3518|In turn these callables are called to build the inputs to the fields of the settings class.
3519|
3520|Each callable should take an instance of the settings class as its sole argument and return a `dict`.
3521|
3522|### Changing Priority
3523|
3524|The order of the returned callables decides the priority of inputs; first item is the highest priority.
3525|
3526|```py
3527|from pydantic import PostgresDsn
3528|
3529|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, PydanticBaseSettingsSource
3530|
3531|
3532|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3533|    database_dsn: PostgresDsn
3534|
3535|    @classmethod
3536|    def settings_customise_sources(
3537|        cls,
3538|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3539|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3540|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3541|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3542|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3543|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3544|        return env_settings, init_settings, file_secret_settings
3545|
3546|
3547|print(Settings(database_dsn='postgres://postgres@localhost:5432/kwargs_db'))
3548|#> database_dsn=PostgresDsn('postgres://postgres@localhost:5432/kwargs_db')
3549|```
3550|
3551|By flipping `env_settings` and `init_settings`, environment variables now have precedence over `__init__` kwargs.
3552|
3553|### Adding sources
3554|
3555|As explained earlier, *pydantic* ships with multiples built-in settings sources. However, you may occasionally
3556|need to add your own custom sources, `settings_customise_sources` makes this very easy:
3557|
3558|```py
3559|import json
3560|from pathlib import Path
3561|from typing import Any
3562|
3563|from pydantic.fields import FieldInfo
3564|
3565|from pydantic_settings import (
3566|    BaseSettings,
3567|    PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3568|    SettingsConfigDict,
3569|)
3570|
3571|
3572|class JsonConfigSettingsSource(PydanticBaseSettingsSource):
3573|    """
3574|    A simple settings source class that loads variables from a JSON file
3575|    at the project's root.
3576|
3577|    Here we happen to choose to use the `env_file_encoding` from Config
3578|    when reading `config.json`
3579|    """
3580|
3581|    def get_field_value(
3582|        self, field: FieldInfo, field_name: str
3583|    ) -> tuple[Any, str, bool]:
3584|        encoding = self.config.get('env_file_encoding')
3585|        file_content_json = json.loads(
3586|            Path('tests/example_test_config.json').read_text(encoding)
3587|        )
3588|        field_value = file_content_json.get(field_name)
3589|        return field_value, field_name, False
3590|
3591|    def prepare_field_value(
3592|        self, field_name: str, field: FieldInfo, value: Any, value_is_complex: bool
3593|    ) -> Any:
3594|        return value
3595|
3596|    def __call__(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
3597|        d: dict[str, Any] = {}
3598|
3599|        for field_name, field in self.settings_cls.model_fields.items():
3600|            field_value, field_key, value_is_complex = self.get_field_value(
3601|                field, field_name
3602|            )
3603|            field_value = self.prepare_field_value(
3604|                field_name, field, field_value, value_is_complex
3605|            )
3606|            if field_value is not None:
3607|                d[field_key] = field_value
3608|
3609|        return d
3610|
3611|
3612|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3613|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file_encoding='utf-8')
3614|
3615|    foobar: str
3616|
3617|    @classmethod
3618|    def settings_customise_sources(
3619|        cls,
3620|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
3621|        init_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3622|        env_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3623|        dotenv_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3624|        file_secret_settings: PydanticBaseSettingsSource,
3625|    ) -> tuple[PydanticBaseSettingsSource, ...]:
3626|        return (
3627|            init_settings,

3630|            file_secret_settings,
3631|        )
3632|
3633|
3634|print(Settings())
3635|#> foobar='test'
3636|```

3707|## In-place reloading
3708|
3709|In case you want to reload in-place an existing setting, you can do it by using its `__init__` method :
3710|
3711|```py
3712|import os
3713|
3714|from pydantic import Field
3715|
3716|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
3717|
3718|
3719|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3720|    foo: str = Field('foo')
3721|
3722|
3723|mutable_settings = Settings()
3724|
3725|print(mutable_settings.foo)
3726|#> foo
3727|
3728|os.environ['foo'] = 'bar'
3729|print(mutable_settings.foo)
3730|#> foo
3731|
3732|mutable_settings.__init__()
3733|print(mutable_settings.foo)
3734|#> bar
3735|
3736|os.environ.pop('foo')
3737|mutable_settings.__init__()
3738|print(mutable_settings.foo)
3739|#> foo
3740|```
3741|
3742|
3743|## Caching settings
3744|
3745|Constructing a settings model reads and validates its configured settings sources each time. This can be costly when
3746|sources read from disk, such as dotenv, secrets, JSON, TOML, or YAML files, or retrieve secrets from cloud secret
3747|managers and parameter stores. Use `settings_cached()` when an application needs one default settings instance per
3748|settings class and process:
3749|
3750|```py
3751|import os
3752|
3753|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
3754|
3755|
3756|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3757|    foo: str = 'foo'
3758|
3759|
3760|settings = Settings.settings_cached()
3761|
3762|print(settings.foo)
3763|#> foo
3764|
3765|os.environ['foo'] = 'bar'
3766|print(Settings.settings_cached().foo)
3767|#> foo
3768|
3769|print(Settings().foo)
3770|#> bar
3771|
3772|Settings.settings_clear_cache()
3773|reloaded_settings = Settings.settings_cached()
3774|
3775|print(reloaded_settings.foo)
3776|#> bar
3777|
3778|os.environ.pop('foo')
3779|Settings.settings_clear_cache()
3780|```
3781|
3782|Calling the settings class directly continues to create a fresh instance. Calling `settings_clear_cache()` removes the
3783|cached instance for that class, so that the next `settings_cached()` call loads the settings sources again.
3784|
3785|Each class is cached under its own key, so a subclass never shares an instance with its parent. This also applies when
3786|clearing: `settings_clear_cache()` only removes the entry for the exact class it is called on. If you reload settings
3787|through a base class, clear each subclass you have cached as well, otherwise those subclasses keep serving their
3788|existing instances.
3789|
3790|The cache is local to each process. The cached object is shared, so any change to it is seen by every caller.
3791|Configuring the model as frozen only prevents assigning to its attributes; it does not freeze the values themselves, so
3792|a mutable field such as a list or dict can still be updated in place and that change is shared process-wide. A cached
3793|instance keeps its own class alive for the lifetime of the process, which is what makes it a singleton. If you build
3794|settings classes dynamically and need them collected, call `settings_clear_cache()` when you are done with one, and its
3795|cache entry is dropped.
3796|
3797|Since `settings_cached` and `settings_clear_cache` are added to `protected_namespaces`, defining a field whose name
3798|starts with either of those raises a `UserWarning`. If you already have such a field, rename it or override
3799|`protected_namespaces` in your model config.
3800|
3801|
3802|## Async environments
3803|
3804|Settings are loaded synchronously. When you use sources that read from disk, such as dotenv, secrets, JSON, TOML, or
3805|YAML files, constructing a settings object in an async application can block the event loop while those files are read.
3806|To load or reload settings from an async context, run the construction in a worker thread:
3807|
3808|```py
3809|import asyncio
3810|from pathlib import Path
3811|
3812|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
3813|
3814|env_path = Path('example.env')
3815|env_path.write_text('api_key=secret\n', encoding='utf-8')
3816|
3817|
3818|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3819|    api_key: str
3820|
3821|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=env_path)
3822|
3823|
3824|async def load_settings() -> Settings:
3825|    return await asyncio.to_thread(Settings)
3826|
3827|
3828|settings = asyncio.run(load_settings())
3829|print(settings.api_key)
3830|#> secret
3831|
3832|env_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
3833|```
3834|
3835|To reload a cached settings object, prefer constructing a fresh instance in a worker thread and swapping the cached
3836|reference, rather than mutating a shared instance in place:
3837|
3838|```py
3839|import asyncio
3840|from pathlib import Path
3841|
3842|from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
3843|
3844|env_path = Path('example.env')
3845|env_path.write_text('api_key=secret\n', encoding='utf-8')
3846|
3847|
3848|class Settings(BaseSettings):
3849|    api_key: str
3850|
3851|    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=env_path)
3852|
3853|
3854|cached_settings = Settings()
3855|
3856|
3857|async def reload_settings() -> None:
3858|    global cached_settings
3859|    cached_settings = await asyncio.to_thread(Settings)
3860|
3861|
3862|asyncio.run(reload_settings())
3863|print(cached_settings.api_key)
3864|#> secret
3865|
3866|env_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
3867|```
3868|
3869|Rebinding the reference is atomic, so concurrent readers always observe a fully-initialized object. By contrast,
3870|[in-place reloading](#in-place-reloading) (`settings.__init__()`) mutates the object while it runs, so a coroutine that
3871|reads the settings during a reload may see partially-updated state; if you rely on it, guard both the reload and every
3872|read with application-level locking.

65|                self.yaml_data, self.yaml_config_section, self.yaml_config_section
66|            )
67|            # An empty section (`section:` with no children) parses to `None`; treat it as an
68|            # empty mapping so it falls back to defaults, mirroring `_read_file`'s `or {}` for
69|            # an empty whole file. A non-mapping section (e.g. a scalar) is a user error, so
70|            # raise a clear message instead of letting `InitSettingsSource` choke on `.keys()`.
71|            if section_data is None:
72|                section_data = {}
73|            elif not isinstance(section_data, dict):
74|                raise TypeError(
75|                    f'yaml_config_section "{self.yaml_config_section}" in {self.yaml_file_path} '
76|                    f'must be a mapping, got {type(section_data).__name__}.'
77|                )
78|            self.yaml_data = section_data
79|        super().__init__(settings_cls, self.yaml_data, _init_state=_init_state)
80|
81|    def _read_file(self, file_path: Path | Traversable) -> dict[str, Any]:
82|        import_yaml()
83|        # Default to UTF-8 rather than the locale encoding, matching `DotEnvSettingsSource`
84|        # and `SecretsSettingsSource`: the YAML spec requires UTF-8/UTF-16, and the locale
85|        # default corrupts (or fails to decode) it on a non-UTF-8 Windows code page.
86|        encoding = self.yaml_file_encoding if self.yaml_file_encoding is not None else 'utf-8'
87|        with file_path.open(encoding=encoding) as yaml_file:
88|            return yaml.safe_load(yaml_file) or {}
89|
90|    def _traverse_nested_section(
91|        self, data: dict[str, Any], section_path: str, original_path: str | None = None
92|    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
93|        """
94|        Traverse nested YAML sections using dot-notation path.
95|
96|        This method tries to match the longest possible key first before splitting on dots,
97|        allowing access to YAML keys that contain literal dot characters.
98|
99|        For example, with section_path="a.b.c", it will try:
100|        1. "a.b.c" as a literal key
101|        2. "a.b" as a key, then traverse to "c"
102|        3. "a" as a key, then traverse to "b.c"
103|        4. "a" as a key, then "b" as a key, then "c" as a key
104|        """
105|        # Track the original path for error messages
106|        if original_path is None:
107|            original_path = section_path
108|
109|        # Only reject truly empty paths
110|        if not section_path:
111|            raise ValueError('yaml_config_section cannot be empty')
112|
113|        # Try the full path as a literal key first (even with leading/trailing/consecutive dots)
114|        try:
115|            return data[section_path]
116|        except KeyError:
117|            pass  # Not a literal key, try splitting
118|        except TypeError as e:
119|            raise TypeError(
120|                f'yaml_config_section path "{original_path}" cannot be traversed in {self.yaml_file_path}. '
121|                f'An intermediate value is not a dictionary.'
122|            ) from e
123|
124|        # If path contains no dots, we already tried it as a literal key above
125|        if '.' not in section_path:
126|            raise KeyError(f'yaml_config_section key "{original_path}" not found in {self.yaml_file_path}')
127|
128|        # Try progressively shorter prefixes (greedy left-to-right approach)
129|        parts = section_path.split('.')
130|        for i in range(len(parts) - 1, 0, -1):
131|            prefix = '.'.join(parts[:i])
132|            suffix = '.'.join(parts[i:])
133|
134|            if prefix in data:
135|                # Found the prefix as a literal key, now recursively traverse the suffix
136|                # The recursive call already raises a `TypeError` carrying `original_path`,
137|                # so let it propagate rather than re-wrapping it in an identical message.
138|                return self._traverse_nested_section(data[prefix], suffix, original_path)
139|
140|        # If we get here, no match was found
141|        raise KeyError(f'yaml_config_section key "{original_path}" not found in {self.yaml_file_path}')
142|
143|    def __repr__(self) -> str:
144|        return f'{self.__class__.__name__}(yaml_file={self.yaml_file_path})'
145|
146|
147|__all__ = ['YamlConfigSettingsSource']

23|class JsonConfigSettingsSource(InitSettingsSource, ConfigFileSourceMixin):
24|    """
25|    A source class that loads variables from a JSON file
26|    """
27|
28|    def __init__(
29|        self,
30|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
31|        json_file: ConfigFileSourceType | None = DEFAULT_PATH,
32|        json_file_encoding: str | None = None,
33|        deep_merge: bool = False,
34|        _init_state: InitState | None = None,
35|    ):
36|        self.json_file_path = json_file if json_file != DEFAULT_PATH else settings_cls.model_config.get('json_file')
37|        self.json_file_encoding = (
38|            json_file_encoding
39|            if json_file_encoding is not None
40|            else settings_cls.model_config.get('json_file_encoding')
41|        )
42|        self.json_data = self._read_files(self.json_file_path, deep_merge=deep_merge)
43|        super().__init__(settings_cls, self.json_data, _init_state=_init_state)
44|
45|    def _read_file(self, file_path: Path | Traversable) -> dict[str, Any]:
46|        # Default to UTF-8 rather than the locale encoding, matching `DotEnvSettingsSource`
47|        # and `SecretsSettingsSource`: RFC 8259 mandates UTF-8 for interchanged JSON, and
48|        # the locale default corrupts (or fails to decode) it on a non-UTF-8 Windows code page.
49|        encoding = self.json_file_encoding if self.json_file_encoding is not None else 'utf-8'
50|        with file_path.open(encoding=encoding) as json_file:
51|            content = json_file.read()
52|        # An empty (or whitespace-only) file is not valid JSON; treat it as an empty
53|        # mapping so it falls back to defaults, mirroring `YamlConfigSettingsSource`'s
54|        # `yaml.safe_load(...) or {}` (and `tomllib`, which returns `{}` for an empty file).
55|        return json.loads(content) if content.strip() else {}

58|        return f'{self.__class__.__name__}(json_file={self.json_file_path})'

1|"""Pyproject TOML file settings source."""
2|
3|from __future__ import annotations as _annotations
4|
5|from pathlib import Path
6|from typing import (
7|    TYPE_CHECKING,
8|)
9|
10|from ..utils import InitState
11|from .toml import TomlConfigSettingsSource
12|
13|if TYPE_CHECKING:
14|    from pydantic_settings.main import BaseSettings
15|
16|
17|class PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource(TomlConfigSettingsSource):
18|    """
19|    A source class that loads variables from a `pyproject.toml` file.
20|    """
21|
22|    def __init__(
23|        self,
24|        settings_cls: type[BaseSettings],
25|        toml_file: Path | None = None,
26|        _init_state: InitState | None = None,
27|    ) -> None:
28|        self.toml_file_path = self._pick_pyproject_toml_file(
29|            toml_file, settings_cls.model_config.get('pyproject_toml_depth', 0)
30|        )
31|        self.toml_table_header: tuple[str, ...] = settings_cls.model_config.get(
32|            'pyproject_toml_table_header', ('tool', 'pydantic-settings')
33|        )
34|        self.toml_data = self._read_files(self.toml_file_path)
35|        for key in self.toml_table_header:
36|            self.toml_data = self.toml_data.get(key, {})
37|        super(TomlConfigSettingsSource, self).__init__(settings_cls, self.toml_data, _init_state=_init_state)
38|
39|    @staticmethod
40|    def _pick_pyproject_toml_file(provided: Path | None, depth: int) -> Path:
41|        """Pick a `pyproject.toml` file path to use.
42|
43|        Args:
44|            provided: Explicit path provided when instantiating this class.
45|            depth: Number of directories up the tree to check for a pyproject.toml.
46|
47|        """
48|        if provided:
49|            return provided.resolve()
50|        rv = Path.cwd() / 'pyproject.toml'
51|        count = 0
52|        if not rv.is_file():
53|            child = rv.parent.parent / 'pyproject.toml'
54|            while count < depth:
55|                if child.is_file():
56|                    return child
57|                if str(child.parent) == rv.root:
58|                    break  # end discovery after checking system root once
59|                child = child.parent.parent / 'pyproject.toml'
60|                count += 1
61|        return rv
62|
63|
64|__all__ = ['PyprojectTomlConfigSettingsSource']

5880|    class Cfg(BaseSettings, cli_ignore_unknown_args=True):
5881|        pos: CliPositionalArg[str]

5886|    # unknown args are always serialized last, even when positionals_first is set.
5887|    cfg = CliApp.run(Cfg, cli_args=['known-pos', '--flag=world', '--', '--unk-opt=1', 'unk-pos'])
5888|    assert cfg.unknown_args == ['--', '--unk-opt=1', 'unk-pos']
5889|
5890|    serialized = CliApp.serialize(cfg, positionals_first=True)
5891|    assert serialized == ['known-pos', '--flag', 'world', '--', '--unk-opt=1', 'unk-pos']
5892|    assert CliApp.run(Cfg, cli_args=serialized) == cfg
5893|

5895|    assert serialized == ['--flag', 'world', 'known-pos', '--', '--unk-opt=1', 'unk-pos']
5896|
5897|    # The known positional is emitted before the marker here, so argparse consumes the marker while looking for it.
5898|    # The known args and the remaining unknown args are preserved, and serialization is stable from here on.
5899|    reparsed = CliApp.run(Cfg, cli_args=serialized)
5900|    assert (reparsed.pos, reparsed.flag) == (cfg.pos, cfg.flag)
5901|    assert reparsed.unknown_args == ['--unk-opt=1', 'unk-pos']
5902|    assert CliApp.serialize(reparsed) == ['--flag', 'world', 'known-pos', '--unk-opt=1', 'unk-pos']

202|def test_settings_cached_loads_unrelated_classes_concurrently(env, clear_settings_cache):
203|    """A class being constructed must not block loading of an unrelated one.
204|
205|    Both classes wait on the same barrier from inside ``__init__``, so this only completes if
206|    they are constructed at the same time. If loading were serialized, the second class would
207|    never start and the barrier would time out.
208|    """
209|    both_constructing = threading.Barrier(2, timeout=10)
210|
211|    class First(BaseSettings):
212|        def __init__(self) -> None:
213|            both_constructing.wait()
214|            super().__init__()
215|
216|    class Second(BaseSettings):
217|        def __init__(self) -> None:
218|            both_constructing.wait()
219|            super().__init__()
220|
221|    def load(settings_cls: type[BaseSettings]) -> BaseSettings:
222|        return settings_cls.settings_cached()
223|
224|    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as executor:
225|        loaded = list(executor.map(load, [First, Second]))
226|
227|    assert [type(instance) for instance in loaded] == [First, Second]

79|    The real lever is the platform locale, which a test cannot portably change: on
80|    CPython the default encoding for ``open()`` is resolved in C and ignores a patched

82|    ``Path.open()`` fall back to cp1252 (a stand-in for any non-UTF-8 Windows code page)
83|    when the caller does not pass an encoding, which is exactly the bug's precondition.
84|
85|    Reads that pass an explicit encoding are untouched, so a source that names its
86|    encoding is unaffected and one that relies on the default is caught on any platform.
87|    """

89|    real_read_text = Path.read_text
90|    real_open = Path.open

92|    def read_text(self: Path, encoding: str | None = None, *args: object, **kwargs: object) -> str:
93|        return real_read_text(self, encoding or fallback, *args, **kwargs)

95|    def open_(
96|        self: Path, mode: str = 'r', buffering: int = -1, encoding: str | None = None, *args: object, **kwargs: object
97|    ) -> IO[Any]:
98|        if 'b' not in mode:
99|            encoding = encoding or fallback
100|        return real_open(self, mode, buffering, encoding, *args, **kwargs)
101|
102|    monkeypatch.setattr(Path, 'read_text', read_text)
103|    monkeypatch.setattr(Path, 'open', open_)
